subjects.subject: The Chateau Frontenac, Quebec City
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower.
expectedBlindAnswer: the castle hotel in Quebec City
expectedBlindAnswerNote: This subject is ALLOWED to demand a place name, unlike the toboggan-run subject below, and the difference
is not a preference: this render is a single non-repeating POI hero that draws one specific building, so a
verifier who cannot name it is reporting a defect in the drawing. The toboggan run is two repeating parallax
tiles that may not carry a landmark at all, so a verifier who names Quebec City from THEM would be reporting
a defect too - in the opposite direction. Ottawa learned that the hard way: its canal contract demanded
"Ottawa" from a tile its own notes forbade putting an Ottawa cue on, and it passed on the verifier's
inference rather than on the art.

mustBeRight.feature: green copper roofs over red-brown brick walls
mustBeRight.why: The single strongest cue and the one a newcomer carries in their head. Green roofs on red-brown brick is the Chateau Frontenac and very little else in Canada. It is also the pair that separates this landmark from Ottawa's: Parliament Hill is green copper over PALE BUFF SANDSTONE, and if both landmarks are drawn in the same stone the game has two buildings that look like each other.
mustBeRight.detail: Use the `copper` ramp for the wing and turret roofs and the `brick` ramp for the walls. `brick` was added to palette.json for this landmark, base hsl(18,52%,44%): MEASURED 2026-09-08 as the hue-filtered median of 106441 sunlit wall pixels in chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg, #a27447 = hsl(29,42%,46%) under low warm autumn sun, against #735749 = hsl(20,21%,37%) for the same wall under overcast winter light in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg. The base sits between them and more saturated, per art-bible section 2. Pale stone banding runs horizontally across the brick; use `stone-light`. NOT grey, NOT sandstone buff for the walls.

mustBeRight.feature: very steep roofs, 60 degrees or more from horizontal
mustBeRight.why: The defining property of the chateau style and the thing that is lost first when a cartoon flattens a roof. A 30 degree roof on this massing is a Victorian hotel, not a chateau, and no amount of green brings it back.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED from the roof silhouette by sky segmentation rather than by eye: the central tower's roof slope is 64.5 and 64.4 degrees on the two sides in chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg (left slope (600,244)->(660,118), right slope (960,139)->(1030,285)), 62.7 degrees in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg, and 60.2 degrees in chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg ((890,376)->(945,280)). The shipped art draws every roof end, gable and lucarne at 62 degrees and the tower roof at 62.3. Anything under 45 degrees stops being a chateau roof.

mustBeRight.feature: one dominant square tower with a pyramidal roof, rising from the centre of a long mass
mustBeRight.why: The composition. Without the tower this reads as a generic Victorian railway hotel - which is what the maskRegion below exists to test, and it is the most useful single thing anyone can measure about this subject.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg (1124x1600), the long-lens near-orthographic elevation, which is the ONE internally consistent view of the three and is therefore the one the drawing is built to. Tower width 161.7 px; total height base(620) to crest(91.7) = 528.3, so WIDTH : HEIGHT = 1 : 3.27. Wing ridge at y=380, so wing height 240 and TOWER : WING = 2.20. Tower standing above the wing ridge = 288.3, which is 0.55 of the total and 1.78 of the tower's width. The other two views bracket these: chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg gives 1:2.85 and 1.84 (oblique, so the tower's width is inflated by seeing two faces), chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg gives 2.30 (close, from below, base hidden behind the wings, so its width:height of 1:1.40 is DISCARDED rather than averaged). The shipped art is 220 x 720 = 1 : 3.27, tower:wing 2.20, 0.55 above the ridge, 1.79 of the width above it. Anything squatter than 1 : 2.5 stops being this tower.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the shipped 1080x900 render: this rectangle covers the tower's finial, its pyramidal roof, the roof's eaves board and the shaft down to the wing ridge at world y 773 (render row 473), and leaves both wings, all four turret cones, every green roof, the brick, the banding, the arcade and the rock untouched. Verified by compositing the mask and looking. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating: it exists to put a number on the claim that the tower is what makes this the Chateau Frontenac rather than a chateau-style hotel, which is otherwise an assertion nobody can check.

mustBeRight.feature: the tower roof is markedly darker than the wing roofs
mustBeRight.why: It is true in every reference here and it is what stops the building reading as one flat green mass. Drawing the tower roof green as well loses the tonal hierarchy that makes the tower dominant.
mustBeRight.detail: The wings and turret cones are green copper; the central tower's roof is a dark slate-grey-green in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg, chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg, chateau-frontenac-tower-2024.jpg and chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg alike. The shipped art uses the `slate` ramp for it against `copper` for the wings.

mustBeRight.feature: conical turrets, several of them, in a rhythm along the mass
mustBeRight.why: The turret count is what makes the building read as a chateau at small size; when everything else has collapsed, the cone silhouette is still there.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED apex angles: 33-36 degrees for the tall corner turrets in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg (three turrets on the right wing at crop x 920-970, 1020-1090 and 1140-1200), and up to 50 degrees for the smaller ones in chateau-frontenac-street-elevation.jpg. The shipped art draws every cone at a 40 degree apex, inside that band. RHYTHM, NOT COUNT (art-bible rule 3): the number of turrets may differ from the photograph; the apex angle and the spacing may not. A cone wider than a 60 degree apex reads as a circus tent and is wrong.

mustBeRight.feature: gabled dormers in a rhythm along the green roofs
mustBeRight.why: It is what stops the long roofs reading as plain green wedges, and it is present in every reference.
mustBeRight.detail: Lucarnes with their own steep gables at the same pitch as the roof, breaking the ridge line, with a small finial. Spacing to width about 1.6, measured on the long wing in chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg (seven dormers at about 45 crop px spacing on 28 crop px width). The number may differ from the photograph; the ratio may not.

mustBeRight.feature: the building stands on rock, above a terrace, not on flat ground
mustBeRight.why: Half of what the photographs show is that this building is on a cliff. Cap Diamant is why the Chateau is where it is, and a chateau on flat ground is a hotel.
mustBeRight.detail: A rock mass in vertical facets under the terrace level, with snow lying on its ledges and a few spruces at its foot. chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg shows the terrace's buttressed retaining wall dropping away below the building; dufferin-terrace-toboggan-slide-1905.jpg shows the same drop from the other side.

simplifyAway: brick coursing and mortar joints
window mullions, transoms and glazing bars
the individual facets of the polygonal turret roofs: four facets read as a cone, sixteen read as noise
balcony ironwork and fire escapes
roof vents, aerials, satellite dishes and the rooftop plant enclosure that sits on the tower's flat deck
the hotel's own signage, awnings and flags: nothing in this level draws lettering of any kind

the corbelled corner bartizans on the tower shaft. DROPPED, NOT APPROXIMATED, and it took three attempts to admit it: at 220 px of tower width a bartizan is a 46 px drum under a 27 px cone and it reads as a brown lozenge stuck to the tower. Art-bible rule 4 is drop, never substitute. The stone quoin strips at the tower's corners, which are also really there, stay and do the job.
neverAdd: a clock face anywhere on this building. There is no clock on the Chateau Frontenac, and a cartoon tower tempts an artist into one; drawing it would also make this landmark and Ottawa's the same landmark
battlements, crenellation or arrow slits: this is an 1893 railway hotel in chateau style, not a fortress, and the difference is the whole point of the roofs
a dome, a minaret, or a second dominant tower
a drawbridge, a portcullis or a moat
the fleur-de-lys or any flag, coat of arms, wordmark or emblem: the game draws no lettering and no heraldry, and a flag on this building would assert something the art has not verified
snow lying in a sheet on the roof planes. At 62 degrees these roofs shed, and every winter reference here shows them clear; snow lies on the ledges, the dormer heads, the cornices and the ground
notes: chateau-frontenac-portrait.jpg is the PRIMARY reference and the only one whose ratios are internally
consistent. Measure against it; use the others to bracket and to sanity-check.
chateau-frontenac-tower-2024.jpg carries no colour profile and its white balance is markedly cool - a
hue-filtered median over its whole facade returns ZERO brick-hued pixels. Use it for geometry only. It is
the same trap as Ottawa's night clock photograph, in a different disguise.
chateau-frontenac-dusk.jpg is a dusk exposure with the building floodlit and coloured architectural lighting
on the tower. Use it for massing and for the roof-slope measurement, never for colour.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise it.
That is the verifier's floor from Ottawa, adopted here rather than re-derived, because no blind pass has been
run on this subject yet. What the size ladder shows as a DRAWING OBSERVATION, which is not an identification:
at 300 px every mustBeRight feature is legible including the lucarne rhythm; at 140 px the lucarnes, the stone
banding and the windows have collapsed to speckle and the read rests entirely on the four cone silhouettes,
the dark central pyramid and the green-on-red contrast. Whether that is still enough is the identifier's call,
not the artist's, and the floor stays at 300 until someone makes it.
The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 1080 x 900 and passed at both probes.
That is what ADR-0013 as amended requires before a landmark ships at 1x rather than the 2x default; the
measured saving is 14.83 MiB -> 3.71 MiB of decoded texture. See assets/style/quebec-city-level.md section 5.

subjects.subject: A toboggan run beside a railed winter promenade
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, terrace above run, the run placed 580 px below the terrace tile's top edge (world y 1280 against 700). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x=0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (2016 and 1440) rather than laying them side by side, and draw the run over the terrace where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. Neither file answers the subject alone: a run with no promenade is a snowy field, and a promenade with no run is a fence. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'terrace', nearMatch: 'slope', nearTop: 580 })`, the same shape and the same offset as the Rideau Canal.
expectedBlindAnswer: a boardwalk and a snow chute
a railed promenade and a snow run
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this list is the whole reason this note exists. Both renders are REPEATING parallax
tiles - 2016 px and 1440 px - so a unique landmark drawn on either appears three or four times across the
level. Nothing on them may name a city, and it follows that nothing may be DEMANDED of them that names one.
Ottawa's canal subject asked its verifier for "Ottawa" from a tile whose own notes forbade drawing the one
landmark that would have said Ottawa; it passed on the verifier's inference from project context rather than
on the art, and had to be amended. That mistake is not repeated here: no answer in this list names Quebec
City, Quebec, the Dufferin Terrace or the Chateau Frontenac, and a verifier who does name one of them is not
wrong - they are just not required to, and the gate must not reward it.
WHERE QUEBEC CITY ACTUALLY COMES FROM: the level composite. `quebec-city-landmark-chateau-frontenac` is a
separate, non-repeating subject that draws one specific building and IS required to be named. The run is where
the player toboggans; the Chateau is what says which city. Splitting them is what lets each be judged on what
it actually contains.

Every answer here is deliberately free of ordinary connectives four letters or longer. "a boardwalk with an ornate railing above a snow slope" was in this list for one run and failed the hand-off's leak scan on the token "with". See the note on quebec-city-riverfront.

mustBeRight.feature: the snow lane is a built chute with edges, not open hillside
mustBeRight.why: This is a toboggan RUN, not a snowy field. The containment is the whole read, exactly as the built edges are what make Ottawa's ice a canal rather than a pond.
mustBeRight.detail: Both references show a chute with high walls and long straight lane dividers running downhill. TrueNorth is a portrait side-scroller and looks ACROSS the run, where the view down it does not exist, so in the side view the containment reads as: a low timber wall running the full width along the far side of the lane with snow capping it, two straight level lane-divider ridges running the full width, and a near snow bank framing the bottom of the frame. Straight, level, parallel edges - a built chute, never a natural slope. AMENDED 2026-09-08 after a genuinely blind pass recorded this feature ABSENT and read the whole lower half as a frozen ice-covered river: the two lane dividers were a boundary between two flat colour bands, which reads as a change of surface, not as a raised ridge. Each divider is now MODELLED - a shaded far flank, a lit crest and a shaded near flank - so it reads as a bank of snow standing above the lane.

mustBeRight.feature: straight parallel runner marks in the lane
mustBeRight.why: A toboggan runner scores STRAIGHT lines. The curved arcs that are correct on skated ice would say skating rink, which is a different level of this game and a different sport.
mustBeRight.detail: Sparse, straight, level, parallel streaks in `snow-light` at 0.30-0.42 opacity, authored as shapes. Never noise, never arcs.

mustBeRight.feature: a promenade above the run with an ornate cast-iron railing
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the run a town amenity rather than a hillside, and the scroll-panel railing is the strongest single piece of built character on these tiles.
mustBeRight.detail: A masonry parapet with a snow-capped coping, and along its head a dark green cast-iron railing of repeating scroll panels between posts with urn finials, drawn from dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg. Two arcs and a ring per bay - rhythm, not tracery.

mustBeRight.feature: globe lamp standards in a rhythm along the promenade
mustBeRight.why: Present in both terrace references and in the 1905 photograph; it is what dates and places the promenade without naming it.
mustBeRight.detail: Dark green columns with a cluster of three white opal globes, one central and two on curved brackets.

mustBeRight.feature: people in winter coats, standing and walking, not skating or skiing
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn small because they are further away and never because they matter less. Winter coats, toques, mitts, boots. No outline: a figure authored into a parallax tile is background. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND on any of them - docs/content-review.md 3.3 outcome 2, and it is a rule here rather than an oversight.

mustBeRight.feature: the lane is PACKED SNOW, and never the `ice` ramp
mustBeRight.why: AMENDED 2026-09-08, and this is the most useful thing anyone has learned about this subject. This entry used to say "use the `ice` ramp for the polished lane against `snow` for the banks", which made the lane the same blue-white ramp as the Rideau Canal Skateway - IN THE SAME HAND-OFF. A blind verifier read the render as a frozen river with wind-blown ice streaks and scored the built-chute feature absent; none of the eight accepted answers is about water, so the subject was not read as a toboggan run at all. Feature 6 was fighting feature 1 and the strongest colour signal won. Correctly drawn runner marks cannot outvote a ramp.
mustBeRight.detail: Use the `snow` ramp for the lane: `snow-base` for the lane body, `snow-light` for the sunlit crests and near lip, `snow-shade` for the flanks and the scored grooves. The `ice` ramp belongs to the Rideau Canal and must not appear anywhere on this lane.

mustBeRight.feature: at least one rider seated on a flat wooden toboggan, on the lane
mustBeRight.why: ADDED 2026-09-08. There was no toboggan and no rider anywhere in 2016 px of this composite, and a blind verifier is being asked to name a sport from an empty surface. The single cheapest thing that says toboggan run is a toboggan on it.
mustBeRight.detail: Seated, knees up, leaning back, one hand on the rope, on a flat wooden deck with a curled front - the posture in quebec-city/toboggan-slide-riders.jpg. Six heads tall in the standing canon, drawn seated. No outline: a figure authored into a parallax tile is background. No cultural marker of any kind.

simplifyAway: individual planks in the boardwalk decking
the cast-iron railing's real tracery: two arcs and a ring per bay is the rhythm, and the rest is below 12 px
street furniture above the lamp line
faces on the background figures below 12 px
neverAdd: the Chateau Frontenac, or any other named or recognisable building, drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles. Scoped deliberately: the Chateau is required on the chateau-frontenac subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building. A prohibition on one subject may not forbid a requirement of another (verifyArtProtocol.contradictionRule), so this one names the tiles it applies to
hockey boards, nets or line markings: this is a slide, not a rink
a ski lift, a chairlift or a tow rope
mountains on the horizon
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language

the `ice` ramp anywhere on the lane. Scoped deliberately: `ice` is required of rideau-canal-skateway and forbidden here, and the reason is that the two subjects are judged in the same hand-off and a shared ramp made one of them read as the other

a recognisable building of any kind on these repeating tiles, INCLUDING street furniture. The terrace tile carried a striped bandstand kiosk with a green-and-white radial roof and a white finial, drawn from quebec-city/dufferin-terrace-boardwalk.jpg, and an unprimed verifier named Terrasse Dufferin, Quebec City off it - from a tile whose own rule this list already was. It is now a plain open timber shelter. The lesson generalises: furniture that is really architecture is architecture
notes: dufferin-terrace-toboggan-slide-1905.jpg is the level's composition reference: the chute, its walls, the
promenade beside it and the crowd, in one frame. toboggan-slide-riders.jpg gives the riders' posture -
seated, knees up, leaning back on a flat wooden toboggan - and the lane structure.
Both historical photographs show timber hoop arches over the run. The shipped tile draws ONE timber
footbridge per 2016 px tile instead: a run of hoops would be overhead in every frame including the one
framing the landmark, and the bridge is the same 'portal the player passes through' that Ottawa validated.
Where it falls, and why it matters: see assets/style/quebec-city-level.md section 3.

BLIND PASS, 2026-09-08. This subject FAILED: the composite read as a frozen ice-covered river, and the built-chute feature was recorded absent. The two causes were in this contract rather than in the drawing - the `ice` ramp on the lane and flat colour-band dividers - and both are corrected above. A previous, primed reading had recorded the same feature PRESENT, which is what a primed reading is worth.

subjects.renderRecipe: UNRENDERED, by decision, and the same decision Ottawa made about its skyline. No source answers this subject. `layer-20-farbank.svg` and `layer-30-river.svg` are a GENERIC winter river town and open water and must stay generic: they are repeating parallax tiles that the low preset drops, and the art bible forbids putting an identifying feature on a droppable layer. A verifier able to name Quebec City from them would be reporting a defect, not a pass. The city's own identifying feature lives in `landmark-chateau-frontenac@1x.svg`, which is judged as `chateau-frontenac`.
subjects.subject: Quebec City seen from across the Saint Lawrence: the Chateau Frontenac on Cap Diamant above the Old Town

mustBeRight.feature: the city stands on a cliff above the river
mustBeRight.why: Cap Diamant is why Quebec City is where it is, and the height is the first thing the view from the water shows.
mustBeRight.detail: A rock bluff with snow on its ledges, rising out of the water, with the town on top rather than beside it.

mustBeRight.feature: the Chateau Frontenac on the skyline, above everything else
mustBeRight.why: From the river it is the one silhouette that names the city.
mustBeRight.detail: Green copper roofs and one dark pyramidal tower, standing clear of the roofline around it. See the chateau-frontenac subject for the measured proportions.

mustBeRight.feature: steep metal roofs on the town below
mustBeRight.why: The vernacular roofline is what places the town in Quebec rather than anywhere else in North America.
mustBeRight.detail: Steep pitched roofs in pale metal with snow on the ridges, dormers, and a parish steeple, packed close. Rhythm, not count.

simplifyAway: individual windows below 6 px
modern towers behind the Old Town
cranes and port machinery
neverAdd: mountains behind the city
a bridge across the river in the same frame as the Old Town
notes: Recorded rather than dropped, so that a later level or a map screen that DOES draw Quebec City from the water
has the contract waiting instead of inventing one. Its lists are dormant while `renders` is empty.

The id avoids ordinary English words on purpose. It was `quebec-city-from-the-river` for one run and the leak scanner in scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs failed the hand-off on the token "from", which the briefing it writes obviously contains. That scanner takes single words from `id` and `expectedBlindAnswer` only, and its own comment says it was narrowed to those because an earlier version fired on "from", "with" and "every" - it assumes those two fields hold only distinctive words. THAT ASSUMPTION IS A CONSTRAINT ON THIS FILE and nothing states it here, so it is stated here: no subject id and no expectedBlindAnswer may contain a common English word of four letters or more. It cost one red run to find.

subjects.subject: The Old Town Clock on Citadel Hill, Halifax
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower and chateau-frontenac.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS ALLOWED TO DEMAND A PLACE NAME. It is a single non-repeating POI hero drawing one
specific building whose stack - white clapboard box, round colonnade, blue-and-gold dial, arched
belfry, green copper ogee dome, gold ball - is not shared by any other building this game will
ever draw. A verifier who cannot name it is reporting a defect in the drawing.
IT IS ALSO THE LEVEL'S ONLY ANCHOR THAT CAN. `pier-21` is the level's other hero and is NOT asked
for a place name; `halifax-quayside` is two repeating tiles and is not asked either. So Halifax
as a place rests on this render alone, which is a deliberate structural choice and is stated here
rather than left to be discovered: if this landmark stops identifying, the level stops being
identifiable, and no amount of work on the other two subjects buys it back.

mustBeRight.feature: a deep blue dial with gold hands and gold marks, on a white drum
mustBeRight.why: The single strongest cue, and the pair that stops this landmark and Ottawa's from being the same landmark. The Peace Tower's dial is WHITE on a buff Gothic sandstone shaft; this one is BLUE on white-painted wood under a green copper dome. Drawn in one colour scheme the two levels would have one clock tower between them.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg (1280x1600, converted from its embedded profile to sRGB before anything was sampled): the dial's centre is at (660, 848), its diameter is about 92 px, and the clock drum it sits on is 185 px wide, so DIAL : DRUM = 0.50. The dial colour is the hue-filtered median of 11500 sunlit dial pixels, #113a7b = hsl(217,76%,27%); `cobalt` was added to palette.json for it at hsl(218,73%,30%), a little lighter so the brass reads at phone size. The shipped art draws the dial at 115 on a 232 drum = 0.496. IT WAS DRAWN AT 0.59 FOR ONE BUILD, on a ratio taken from a colour segmentation that the sky above and the flanking sash windows either side were both contaminating; the number that stuck was read off a labelled grid crop of the same file, where what is being measured can be seen.

mustBeRight.feature: a green copper ogee dome under a small balustraded cupola and a gold ball
mustBeRight.why: The top of the silhouette, and the second thing a person uses to recognise it. A hemispherical dome or a pointed spire in its place changes the building.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED by copper-hue segmentation on halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg, which is the one measurement on this subject a segmentation could make cleanly because nothing else in the frame is that hue: the dome occupies rows 600..700 and columns 567..751, so 185 wide by 100 tall - HEIGHT : WIDTH = 0.54, and WIDTH = 0.298 of the base building. It is an ogee, wider below than at the crown, not a hemisphere. Above it a short white cupola with a balustrade, and one gold ball finial about 0.05 of the base width.

mustBeRight.feature: an open arched belfry with bells, between the dial and the dome
mustBeRight.detail: A white octagonal stage with round-arched openings, the centre one wider than the two flanking it, and two bells visible inside. MEASURED: it occupies rows 700..788 and is about 150 px wide, which is 0.242 of the base building's width - NARROWER than the drum below it (0.298) and than the dome above it (0.298), and that pinch is what makes the stack read as a stack.

mustBeRight.feature: a round colonnaded gallery below the dial, wider than every stage above it
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the building classical rather than ecclesiastical, and it is the stage this drawing got wrong twice - 29 per cent too narrow on the first build and 15 per cent too WIDE on the correction, because the correction's denominator was contaminated. It is now measured off a grid crop.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: the gallery's elliptical roof rim runs x 497..822 at row 935, so it is 325 px wide, which is 0.524 of the base building's width (620 px, x 357..977 at row 1150). The column ring inside it is 307 px. Against 0.298 for the clock drum above. A ring of plain columns - six read correctly; the number may differ from the photograph, the width may not - under a green copper rim, around a smaller white drum with one window.

mustBeRight.feature: white painted wood, not stone and not brick
mustBeRight.detail: Every wall on this building is white-painted clapboard on a stone rubble plinth. Use the `white` ramp for the walls and `path` for the plinth. NOT `stone` (that is Nepean sandstone and belongs to Parliament Hill) and NOT `brick`.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands on a grassy slope, not on a street or a plaza
mustBeRight.why: The hill is half of why the building is where it is and half of what a photograph of it shows. On flat paving it reads as a town hall.
mustBeRight.detail: A turf slope running under the stone plinth, with the ground falling away either side. halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg shows the glacis behind and below it; halifax/town-clock-1948.jpg shows the same slope from above with the town and the harbour beyond.

mustBeRight.feature: proportion: a wide low base carrying a tall narrow stack
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED against the base building's width, which is the one unambiguous quantity in the picture: base width 620 px (x 357..977 at row 1150); total height from the top of the gold ball (row 548) to the foot of the plinth (row 1310) 762 px, so WIDTH : HEIGHT = 1 : 1.23. Everything above the base roof (rows 548..1090) is 542 px = 0.874 of the base width. The shipped art is 738 x 953 = 1 : 1.29 with 0.894 above the roof, both inside the plus-or-minus 10 per cent band. Anything taller than 1 : 1.6 stops being this building and becomes a steeple.

simplifyAway: clapboard boarding: it is a surface pattern, and art-bible section 1 forbids drawing one
glazing bars: a twelve-pane sash becomes one dark pane with one cross, which is rhythm replacing count
Roman numerals on the dial: at 137 px a numeral is 9 px, so they become four cardinal marks. The same substitution Ottawa made on the Peace Tower, for the same reason
the individual balusters of the cupola rail below 8 px

the Citadel's signal mast and whatever flag is flying from it. It stands behind the clock in halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg and it is really there, but at cartoon scale a bare mast is a line and a drawn flag would assert something this project has not verified (OQ-ART-04)
the mouldings, dentils and brackets of the cornices: each becomes one flat band
the stone rubble coursing of the plinth: four flat marks, not a pattern
neverAdd: a pointed spire, a Gothic arch or any tracery ON THIS BUILDING. Scoped deliberately: a Gothic arch is required of peace-tower and forbidden here, and the reason is that this is a Palladian tower of 1803, not a Gothic Revival one
a cross, a weathervane or any religious emblem: it is not a church, and a cross on the cupola is the single most likely wrong addition
battlements, crenellation or arrow slits
a flag, a coat of arms, a wordmark or any lettering
brick or stone walls above the plinth
a second dial on the same visible face
notes: halifax/town-clock-elevation.jpg is the PRIMARY reference and the only one measured. It is a long
street view in full sun, near-orthographic, with the whole building in frame, and it is the one

HOW THESE NUMBERS WERE TAKEN, because it matters on this photograph. Automated segmentation works for the dome, whose copper hue is unique in the frame, and FAILS everywhere else: the sky is a pale low-saturation blue that a white mask catches, the hillside behind the building is bright, and the drum's flanking sash windows and the gold hands both cut a blue mask. Three widths were wrong before this was noticed. The figures above are read off a LABELLED GRID CROP of the same file - the crop, its offsets and its scale are in scratch/gen/, and anyone can regenerate it - which is slower and is the only method here whose errors are visible while you are making them.
internally consistent view of the three.
halifax/town-clock-close-elevation.jpg is closer and from below, so its vertical proportions are
foreshortened, and its white balance is warm dusk - the grass reads brown. Use it for the belfry,
the bells and the window layout. NEVER for colour and never for a height ratio.
halifax/town-clock-1948.jpg is public domain and shows the clock from Citadel Hill with the town
and the harbour behind, which is the level's own composition. Its dial is WHITE: the dial was
repainted blue with gold later, and the level draws today's building. Use it for the setting.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to
recognise it. That is the verifier's floor from Ottawa, adopted rather than re-derived, because no
blind pass has been run on this subject and the artist does not set the threshold for their own
work. What the size ladder shows as a DRAWING OBSERVATION and explicitly not an identification: at
200 px every mustBeRight feature is still legible, including the two bells and the gold ball.
The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 800 x 1010 and passed at
both probes, which is what ADR-0013 as amended requires before a landmark ships at 1x rather than
the 2x default. The measured saving is 12.32 MiB -> 3.08 MiB of decoded texture.

subjects.subject: The immigration and ocean terminal buildings at Pier 21, Halifax
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswer: a pier shed and an ocean liner
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS DELIBERATELY NOT ASKED FOR A PLACE NAME, and the reason is a property of the
building rather than of the drawing. Pier 21 is a brick shed. Its one unmistakable feature in every
photograph is the name PAINTED ON IT, and a round emblem beside the name - and this project draws
no lettering anywhere, for a reason that has nothing to do with this level: make verify-art refuses
any render source containing a <text> element, because a name drawn into the picture defeats every
byte-level leak check in the hand-off. Strip the name and what is left is a three-storey brick
block with a streamlined entrance, which is a building type and not a place.
SO THE GENERIC ANSWERS PASS. `Pier 21` and `Halifax` stay in the list because a verifier who names
them is not wrong - the liner, the terminal block and the immigrant train together are a fair
inference - but they are NOT required, and the gate must not reward them. Ottawa's canal subject
demanded a city name from a tile its own notes forbade putting a city cue on, passed on the
verifier's inference from project context, and had to be amended afterwards. The PO flagged this
one in advance and declined to write an expectedBlindAnswer for it. This is the answer to that:
draw the shed accurately, ask it only for what it can carry, and put the level's place-identity on
`town-clock`, which can.
One answer was removed from this list before it ever ran: "a port terminal". The hand-off's
leak scanner takes single words of four letters or more out of `id` and `expectedBlindAnswer`
and refuses any handed-over text containing one, and the briefing it writes contains the word
"important". `quebec-city-riverfront`'s note states the rule as "no common English word of
four letters or more"; the real rule is narrower and nastier - no word that is a SUBSTRING of
any word in the briefing. Checked mechanically against the real `leakTokens` before shipping.

mustBeRight.feature: a three-storey red brick block with a flat stone-coped parapet
mustBeRight.why: It is the building. Everything else in the frame is context for it.
mustBeRight.detail: Red-brown facing brick with a pale stone coping at the parapet, one stone band below the coping and one string course at mid height, and a rhythm of rectangular sash windows with stone sills, three storeys of them. MEASURED on halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg, converted to sRGB first: the hue-filtered median of 104302 sunlit brick pixels is #c07e70 = hsl(11,39%,60%). That is a LIGHTER, REDDER brick than the Chateau Frontenac's, whose sunlit median is hsl(29,42%,46%). The shipped art uses the existing `brick` ramp anyway, whose light tone is hsl(25,52%,59%) - the same lightness, 14 degrees more orange. A second near-identical brick ramp was rejected: the two buildings are in different levels and never on screen together, and the palette does not need two reds to say brick. The departure is recorded here rather than hidden.

mustBeRight.feature: a pale streamlined entrance standing proud of the brick
mustBeRight.why: It is the one piece of architecture on the building that is not a shed, and it is what dates it. Without it the block is a warehouse.
mustBeRight.detail: A pale rendered pylon with rounded corners, a curved cantilevered canopy over the doorway and a small balcony with a plain pipe rail above it. Drawn from halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg. NOT a classical portico, NOT columns.

mustBeRight.feature: long low pier sheds running away on both sides
mustBeRight.why: A terminal is a shed with a small building attached, not a building on its own, and the length is the whole character of the place.
mustBeRight.detail: Two-storey sheds with shallow roofs carrying a raised monitor along the ridge, a rhythm of small windows, and walls markedly paler than the brick. They run off both edges of the frame: the real shed is over 350 m long and nothing in a portrait frame can show that except by leaving.

mustBeRight.feature: an ocean liner berthed alongside, rising above the shed roof
mustBeRight.why: The ship is what a pier shed is FOR, and it is the difference between this render and a row of warehouses. halifax/pier-21-liner-1934.jpg shows exactly this: a three-funnelled liner alongside the shed, taller than everything on the pier.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark hull with a red boot band, a white superstructure with window bands and a row of boats along the boat deck, two buff funnels with dark tops, and one plain mast. Generic: no line's livery, no name, no house flag. Two funnels rather than three - the count may differ from the photograph, the massing may not.

mustBeRight.feature: a railway coach standing on a track in front of the building
mustBeRight.why: People who arrived here left by train, and the track runs along the pier apron in every reference. It is drawn because halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg shows a preserved coach standing exactly there, not because a train would be a nice idea.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark green heritage passenger coach on rails and sleepers, with a window rhythm, a brass stripe under the windows and two trucks. No lettering, no number, no reporting mark.

simplifyAway: brick coursing and mortar joints
window glazing bars: one dark pane with one horizontal bar
the fire escapes, downpipes, roof vents and modern plant on the shed roofs
the parapet's brick corbelling and the moulded stone profiles: each becomes one flat band
the coach's underframe detail, couplers, steps and roof vents
neverAdd: the painted name on the parapet, in any size or language, or any other lettering anywhere in the level. It is what the building is known by and it is the one thing this project cannot draw

the round emblem beside the name on the brick face: it is the operating institution's mark, and an approximated mark is worse than none - the same reasoning art-bible section 10 applies to the officer's insignia
a clock face on this building. There is no clock here; the round sign is a sign, and drawing it as a clock would make this landmark and Ottawa's and Halifax's own Town Clock all the same landmark
a flag, a coat of arms or a house flag on the liner
a lighthouse, a fort or a bridge in the same frame: none of them is at Pier 21
notes: halifax/pier-21-entrance.jpg is CC BY 3.0 and is the primary reference for the brick block, the
streamlined entrance, the stone banding and the coach. It is an oblique view, so it is a reference
for elements and colour and NOT for a width-to-height ratio.
halifax/pier-21-liner-1934.jpg is public domain, is an aerial, and is the reference for the shed's
length, the liner alongside and the covered gangway. It is also the only reference showing what the
place was built to do.
halifax/pier-21-and-the-seaport.jpg is public domain, small and low contrast. It is here for one
thing: it shows how completely the painted name carries the building's identity, which is the
finding this subject's expectedBlindAnswerNote rests on.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: 300 px wide, adopted from Ottawa as above. The shipped source is 900 x 620.

subjects.subject: A timber harbour boardwalk running past working wharves
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the town above the quayside, the quayside placed 160 px below the town tile's top edge (world y 860 against 700). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 2016) rather than laying them side by side, and draw the quayside over the town where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. Neither file answers the subject alone: a town with no waterfront is a town, and a boardwalk with nothing behind it is a fence. `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'uptown', nearMatch: 'quayside', nearTop: 160 })`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both renders are REPEATING parallax tiles - 1800 px and 2016 px - so a unique
landmark drawn on either appears three or four times across the level. Nothing on them may name a
city, and it follows that nothing may be DEMANDED of them that names one. No answer in this list
names Halifax, Nova Scotia, the Citadel or Pier 21, and a verifier who does name one of them is
not wrong - they are just not required to, and the gate must not reward it.
WHERE HALIFAX ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `town-clock`, a separate non-repeating POI hero that IS
required to be named. The boardwalk is where the player walks; the clock is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: a planked timber deck with a low kerb at the water's edge
mustBeRight.why: It is a BOARDWALK, not a quay and not a street. The planking and the timber edge are the whole read, exactly as the built edges are what make Ottawa's ice a canal rather than a pond.
mustBeRight.detail: The boards run ACROSS the view, so the lines between them are horizontal. They were drawn as vertical separators for one composite and read as a picket fence, and then as horizontal hairlines on a flat grey field and read as a PAVED STREET - a blind pass called the composite a waterfront main street and reached no accepted answer. Both failures came from this line, so it now says what makes a deck read as a deck rather than what colour it is. FOUR THINGS, all of them required. (1) Board courses of graded depth, the nearer ones taller, none thinner than 12 px, separated by a dark gap and a lit chamfer on the near board - the gaps between the boards are the strongest lines on the deck. (2) BOARD ENDS: butt joints at a regular period, staggered between courses, thin and quiet - drawn at the weight of the gaps they turn the deck into a brick wall. (3) Enough tone difference between adjacent boards to read as timber rather than as a poured surface, and warm: weathered timber is a warm grey-tan, and the `path` ramp alone is concrete. Author the deck from `stone-light` with `path-light` and `stone-base` boards through it and `path-shade` in the gaps. (4) A visible deck edge: a low timber kerb along the far edge with a lighter sunlit top, a dark underside so it stands proud of the deck, its cast shadow on the deck below it, and the deck's own shadow on the water in the open slips.

mustBeRight.feature: ornate dark lamp standards, bollards and benches along the water's edge
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the deck a public promenade rather than a working pier, and it is the strongest built rhythm on these tiles.
mustBeRight.detail: Tall dark posts with a single white globe, drawn from halifax/waterfront-boardwalk.jpg; squat rounded mooring bollards; timber benches with dark ends. Everything the boardwalk carries stands at the FAR edge, so the deck nearest the camera stays clear for the player.

mustBeRight.feature: open slips of water between the wharves, with moored hulls
mustBeRight.why: Half of a working waterfront is the water between the wharves, and a boardwalk with no water in the frame is a street.
mustBeRight.detail: Short bands of harbour water between the buildings, with a moored sailing hull and masts, and a tug with a dark hull and a white wheelhouse. Generic: no name, no livery, no house flag.

mustBeRight.feature: low waterfront buildings with steep gables and dormers
mustBeRight.detail: Two- and three-storey buildings with steep pitched roofs, dormer rhythm and shopfronts at the foot, plus one timber cargo shed with big doors and a monitor roof. Rhythm, not count.

mustBeRight.feature: people walking, to the same cartoon proportions as every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures in a parallax tile are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn small because they stand further from the camera and never because they matter less. Summer clothes. No outline: a figure authored into a parallax tile is background. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND on any of them - docs/content-review.md 3.3 outcome 2, applied deliberately rather than by omission.

mustBeRight.feature: gulls
mustBeRight.detail: A few white gulls on the bollards and in the air. Small, flat, two tones and a beak. They are the one thing on these tiles that says salt water rather than river.

simplifyAway: individual planks below 12 px. AMENDED 2026-09-08: this used to end "and every plank end", and the board ends are now REQUIRED by the first `mustBeRight` entry. A deck with no board ends is a floor of infinitely long planks, which is what a poured surface looks like
the pile cribbing under the deck: it is below the level's ground line and is never drawn
rigging, shrouds and sails on the moored hulls: a mast and one crosstree is the rhythm
faces on the background figures below 12 px
street furniture above the lamp line
neverAdd: any named or recognisable building drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles. Scoped deliberately: the Town Clock is required on the town-clock subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language
a lighthouse: Peggy's Cove is not in Halifax and is not this level
snow, ice or bare winter trees: this level is summer, and two of this game's other levels are already winter
mountains on the horizon
notes: halifax/waterfront-boardwalk.jpg is CC BY 2.0 and is the primary composition reference: the deck,
the lamps, the benches, the bollards and the interpretive panel in one frame. It is heavily
processed - dark, high contrast, a storm sky - so it is a reference for GEOMETRY only and never
for colour.
halifax/waterfront-and-skyline.jpg and halifax/waterfront-harbour.jpg are CC0 and are the colour
and massing references: the timber wharves, the low waterfront buildings, the slips and the town
rising behind them.
BLIND PASS, 2026-09-08. This subject FAILED. Every `mustBeRight` feature was drawn and none of
`neverAdd` was present; the identifier read the composite as a small coastal town's waterfront main
street and reached none of the seven accepted answers. The single cause was the DECK: a flat grey
field with three hairline separators, no board ends, no visible edge. The cause was in this contract
and not in the drawing - `grey weathered planking` is a true description of a boardwalk and also a
true description of a pavement, and the drawing obeyed it. The first `mustBeRight` entry above now
describes the structure instead, and the deck is redrawn to it: graded board courses, staggered butt
joints on a 336 px period that tiles at the 2016 px seam with the straddling board given one tone at
both ends, warm board-to-board tone variation, and a modelled timber edge with its shadow on the deck
and on the water. Nothing else on the tile changed: no landmark was added and none may be, for the
reason in `expectedBlindAnswerNote`. Judged by rendering the composite and looking at it, three times,
not by reading the SVG.

subjects.subject: The CN Tower, Toronto
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: ALLOWED to demand a place name, on the same test `chateau-frontenac` passes: a single
non-repeating POI hero drawing one specific structure. It is the only thing in the Toronto level
that names a city - `toronto-trail` is two repeating tiles and is generic on purpose.

mustBeRight.feature: one wide observation pod about three fifths of the way up a very slender shaft
mustBeRight.why: The composition, and the thing that makes this a tower and not a mast. The maskRegion below exists to put a number on how much of the identification it carries.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on toronto/cn-tower-skyline-elevation.jpg (1600x1012) by thresholding the tower against the sky row by row. EVERY FIGURE IS IN MAIN POD WIDTHS, not in fractions of the total height, and that is deliberate: the tower's base is hidden behind the waterfront in this view and in every other reference here, so a ratio against the total height would have an unmeasured denominator - the mistake ADR-0014 records for the Chateau, in a different disguise. Pod maximum width 45 px at row 402. Shaft immediately below the pod 14 px, so SHAFT : POD = 1 : 3.2. Mast tip at row 207, so tip to pod centre = 195 = 4.33 pod widths. Shaft at row 554 is 18 px and the base flare begins about row 640, 5.3 pod widths below the pod centre. The shipped art is a 97 px pod with a 29 px shaft (1 : 3.3), 4.33 pod widths of mast, and the flare at 5.3. Anything with a shaft thicker than 1 : 2.5 stops being this tower.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the shipped 700x1020 render: this rectangle covers the whole observation pod - the deck ring, both dark glass bands and the white radome - and leaves the mast, the smaller upper pod, the shaft, the splayed base, the domed stadium and the glazed block untouched. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating. The Chateau's masked probe dropped 0.80 to 0.35 and the Peace Tower's only 0.92 to 0.80, and the difference told us the Chateau identifies by ensemble and the Peace Tower by two hard tokens. This subject looks like a two-token one - the pod and the dome at its foot - and the mask is how that gets checked instead of assumed.

mustBeRight.feature: the pod's widest element is a fat white ring below its glass bands
mustBeRight.why: It is the single most distinctive thing about the pod and it is what a cartoon flattens away first, leaving a plain disc on a stick.
mustBeRight.detail: From top to bottom: a pale metal deck ring, a dark glass band, a pale ring, a second dark glass band, then a WHITE torus that is wider than all of them, then a dark under-deck. Drawn from toronto/cn-tower-pod.jpg.

mustBeRight.feature: a second, much smaller pod higher up the shaft
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: at row 310 the shaft widens to 16 px against the main pod's 45, so the upper pod is 0.36 of the main pod's width, and it sits 2.04 pod widths above the main pod's centre. It is small and it is not optional: without it the tower is a single-pod tower, which is a different building.

mustBeRight.feature: a long tapering antenna mast above the pod
mustBeRight.detail: About four pod widths of mast above the pod centre, tapering to a point. DELIBERATE EXAGGERATION, and the only one on this subject: in the best reference here the mast is TWO TO THREE PIXELS wide, at the resolution limit of the photograph, which is 5 px at the size shipped and gone at the 25 per cent probe. It is drawn at 0.155 of the pod width at its base and 0.06 at the tip. Exaggerating an identifying feature is simplification (art-bible 5.2); adding one is invention.

mustBeRight.feature: a tapered concrete shaft that splays into legs at its foot
mustBeRight.detail: Warm pale grey concrete, not steel and not glass. The shaft is a hexagonal prism in life; in elevation it reads as one tapering mass with two darker vertical strips for the ribs. At the bottom it splays out into legs - it is not a cylinder standing on the ground.

mustBeRight.feature: a low white domed stadium at the tower's foot
mustBeRight.why: CONTEXT, drawn because it is really there and is in front of the tower from the water in every wide reference here, and because it is what separates this render from a generic concrete communications tower. The same role Centre Block's wings play for the Peace Tower.
mustBeRight.detail: A shallow white dome on a low ring wall, its top about a sixth of the tower's height, standing in FRONT of the tower's base and hiding part of it. Its width is about a third of the tower's height. No roof panel joints, no retractable roof segments, no lettering.

simplifyAway: the external elevator tracks and their glass fronts
the pod's coloured architectural lighting and any red band: it is programmable and changes nightly, so drawing one state asserts a state
the glass floor and the outdoor walk platform
the third rib of the shaft: two shaded strips read as a ribbed shaft, three read as noise
aerials, dishes and the plant on the mast
the stadium's roof panel joints, its hotel windows and its ring-wall structure below 12 px
neverAdd: lattice steelwork or guy wires: it is a free-standing reinforced concrete tower and drawing it as a guyed lattice mast is the single most likely wrong simplification
a second observation pod at the same level, a crown, a spire or a dome ON THE TOWER
a revolving restaurant sign, a wordmark or any lettering anywhere in the level
a flag on the mast
a clock face: there is no clock, and this game already has two clock towers
notes: toronto/cn-tower-skyline-elevation.jpg is CC0, is the PRIMARY reference and is the only one
measured: a long-distance view from the islands, so it is near-orthographic and the whole tower is
in frame. Its base is hidden behind the waterfront, which is why every ratio here is against the
pod's width rather than against the total height.
toronto/cn-tower-pod.jpg is CC BY 3.0 and is the reference for the pod's bands and the radome.
It is a close view from below, so it is a reference for the band ORDER and nothing else.
toronto/cn-tower-shaft.jpg is CC0, is an extreme worm's-eye view, and is here for the concrete's
colour and the ribbed shaft. It is useless for any proportion at all.
toronto/skyline-overcast.jpg is CC0 and shows the tower small against a flat overcast sky, which
is the closest thing here to how it reads at the size ladder's lower rungs.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: 300 px wide, adopted from Ottawa. The shipped source is 700 x 1020, and the tower
itself is 97 px wide at its widest - so the floor is about the FILE, not the shaft, and a level
that scales this landmark down loses the upper pod first and the mast second.
The two-size test was run at the shipping size and passed at both probes: at 25 per cent the pod,
the upper pod, the mast and the dome all survive, and the 120 px silhouette is a needle with one
bulge and a dome at its foot.

subjects.subject: A separated cycling path along a city waterfront, under a downtown skyline
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the skyline above the boulevard, the boulevard placed 340 px below the skyline tile's top edge (world y 900 against 560). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1440), and draw the boulevard over the skyline where they overlap. Neither file answers the subject alone: a skyline with no street is a skyline, and a path with nothing behind it is a path. `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'skyline', nearMatch: 'boulevard', nearTop: 340 })`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: AMENDED 2026-09-08, and the amendment is two words long. A blind pass answered "a generic modern
city street with a protected bicycle lane" and FAILED, because every accepted form of the word was
a contraction - bike, cycle, cycle track - and none was `bicycle`. The art was not at fault: every
`mustBeRight` entry was found on the tile and the answer describes what is drawn. So `a bicycle lane`
and `a protected bicycle lane` now pass. `protected` is accepted because the separation IS drawn and
is a `mustBeRight` entry of its own - a verifier who names it has seen more of the tile, not less.
This is the same amendment `rideau-canal-skateway` needed and it was found the same way, so state the
general rule once: an `expectedBlindAnswer` list is a VOCABULARY for one picture, and a list that
omits the plain word for the thing drawn measures the verifier's diction rather than the art. It is
widened to the honest answer and no further - nothing here accepts a footpath, a road or a pavement.
GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this one has teeth: the skyline tile is the layer the LOW preset keeps,
so it is the most-seen art in the level, and it is precisely the layer that may not carry a
recognisable building. Every tower on it is a plain mass. A verifier who names Toronto from these
two tiles would be reporting a defect, not a pass.
WHERE TORONTO ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `cn-tower`, a separate non-repeating POI hero. The trail is
where the player rides; the tower is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: an asphalt path carrying a green line and a blue line along its length
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes the path a signed cycling route rather than a footpath, and the paired coloured lines are the strongest single piece of built character on these tiles.
mustBeRight.detail: Two flat longitudinal stripes, one green and one blue, running the full width of the tile, drawn from toronto/waterfront-trail.jpg where they run the length of the waterfront path. Straight, level and parallel.

mustBeRight.feature: a white bicycle mark and a direction arrow painted on the surface
mustBeRight.why: It is what says BIKE rather than footpath, and it is the only symbol in the level.
mustBeRight.detail: Two wheels, a frame, bars and a saddle, flat white, drawn as shapes from toronto/bike-lane-street.jpg. A road marking, not a sign. There is no lettering anywhere in this level.

mustBeRight.feature: a planted verge and a kerb separating the path from the road
mustBeRight.why: The separation is the whole point of the facility, and a lane painted at the edge of traffic is a different and more dangerous thing to depict.
mustBeRight.detail: A strip of grass with a sunlit top edge and a pale kerb along the far side of the path.

mustBeRight.feature: young street trees, slim rather than mature
mustBeRight.detail: Recent plantings about twice head height with a narrow canopy, not a spreading avenue tree. toronto/waterfront-trail.jpg shows exactly this: thin trunks in a grass strip. Drawing them as mature maples would put the path in a park.

mustBeRight.feature: people riding, to the same cartoon proportions as every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures in a parallax tile are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn small because they are across the path. Helmets rather than hairstyles, because the level's locomotion is a bike. No outline. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND - docs/content-review.md 3.3 outcome 2.

mustBeRight.feature: a dense downtown skyline of tall towers behind
mustBeRight.detail: Plain rectangular masses in pale concrete, dark glass and blue-green glass, with flat tops, crowns, setbacks and plant enclosures, standing out of an opaque haze band. Rhythm and massing only.

simplifyAway: individual windows on the towers: a horizontal band rhythm, never a grid of panes
traffic signals, hydro poles and overhead wires
parked cars and moving traffic
the bike-share operator's livery on the bicycles in the rack: they are drawn in palette colours and carry no operator colour and no dock branding
kerb ramps, drainage and tactile paving
neverAdd: any named or recognisable building drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles, and the CN Tower above all: it is required on the cn-tower subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language
a streetcar, a bus or a train in the cycling lane
mountains on the horizon: this city is on a lake plain
snow or winter trees: this level is late summer
notes: toronto/waterfront-trail.jpg is CC0 and is the primary reference: the separated path, the green
and blue lines, the grass verge, the young trees and the bike rack in one frame.
toronto/bike-lane-street.jpg is CC BY 2.0, from the Ontario government, and is the reference for
the green surface treatment, the white bicycle mark and the arrow. Its required credit line is in
the `author` field of its entry in assets/credits.json, which is where a licence condition of that
kind has to live: credits.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and has no other field for it.
toronto/skyline-overcast.jpg is CC0 and is the massing reference for the tower rhythm.

subjects.renderRecipe: A CHARACTER IS NEVER JUDGED FROM ONE FILE. Composite onto a 240 x 470 canvas: take `parts` from assets/style/rig-contract.json in `z` order, resolve each `frame` template with the costume named below and any skin, hairShape, hairColour, headCovering, feature and expression, and draw each part at its own viewBox origin, mirroring the parts whose `mirrorX` is true about x=120. A resolved template absent from `frames` draws nothing, which is how the human artboards get no tail. The guide gets no toque a different way and the difference matters when you build the recipe: `head-covering-toque` IS in `frames`, and since `headCovering` falls back to `toque` the officer and the guide pin `headCovering: none` in their artboard `skins`. Resolve slots artboard-skins-first, then fallback, or you will hand the identifier a Mountie in a bobble hat. Every listed file is unidentifiable alone; a sleeve is a blue capsule. Use costume=beaver and leave every other slot at its fallback: head-skin and hair-crop ARE drawn and are then covered entirely by head-shell-beaver, which is why no pelt tone was added to the skin slot, and a composite that omits them is not what ships. Vary the expression between runs. THE HAND-OFF MUST CONTAIN THE PLAYER BESIDE THE GUIDE on one canvas, for the same reason the officer's does: identical proportions cannot be judged from one figure.
subjects.subject: A cartoon North American beaver, standing upright, as a companion guide

mustBeRight.feature: the paddle tail, visible and out to one side
mustBeRight.why: One of the two features that carry the identification, and one that is carried out to the side rather than behind, because anything drawn behind a torso is not drawn at all. Since the guide turned to face its direction of travel, the wearer right side is the TRAILING side, so the paddle streams out behind a moving animal. If it disappears first at small size, it is drawn too small or too dark.
mustBeRight.detail: A broad flat oval leaning down and away from the wearer's right hip, on a stub that leaves the body at the hip and tucks behind the leg, with three cross bands for scale and a large lit upper face. About 100 x 130 px in character space.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the 240x470 composite the renderRecipe builds: this rectangle covers the whole tail, stub and paddle, and leaves the head, body, forelimbs and the near hind leg untouched. It exists so the claim that the tail is load-bearing has a test - mask it and the identification should degrade.
mustBeRight.maskRegionNote: The tail window in character space. DIAGNOSTIC, never gating. guide.md 3 calls the paddle one of the two features that make a beaver identifiable at phone size; with it painted out, what is left is the muzzle and the incisors, and the answer says which of the two is doing the work.

mustBeRight.feature: two large incisors below the mouth
mustBeRight.why: The other load-bearing feature, and the one that reads at the smallest sizes.
mustBeRight.detail: Two white teeth, together about 36 px wide and 20 tall in character space, hanging below the shared mouth line on a pale snout pad.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: MEASURED against the same composite: covers both incisors and the lower snout pad and leaves the eyes, brows, ears and body alone.

mustBeRight.feature: ONE small ear, set high and well BACK on the skull
mustBeRight.why: This is the difference between a beaver and a bear, and the first version of this head got it wrong: high, large, rounded ears read as a bear in the render even though the teeth and tail were already right.
mustBeRight.detail: Small, dark, rounded, mostly inside the head silhouette, high and well back - which is where beaver-head-and-forepaws.jpg and beaver-alberta-profile.jpg put it. ONE, not two: the head is turned and a turned head shows one ear, and two is the loudest front-view signal there is. Ears that stand clear of the skull read as a bear; that has been drawn wrong twice now, high and round the first time and large and paired the second.

mustBeRight.feature: a broad blunt muzzle with a wide flat nose
mustBeRight.detail: A pale snout pad filling the lower half of the face with a wide dark nose across its top.

mustBeRight.feature: a pale belly against a darker pelt
mustBeRight.detail: Ventral fur a full ramp lighter than the flank.

mustBeRight.feature: webbed hind feet
mustBeRight.detail: Bare dark hide, a single rounded wedge with three toe notches, a tone lighter than the tail so the two dark masses do not merge at phone size.

mustBeRight.feature: the figure is TURNED TOWARD THE DIRECTION IT TRAVELS
mustBeRight.why: This is a portrait 2D side-scroller and every character in it walks, skates, toboggans or bikes ALONG the screen. A character drawn front-on, facing the viewer, is wrong by construction - it reads as a menu portrait somebody slid sideways - and that is what the repository owner reported from the live site: that it is looking at the user. A verifier who describes the figure as facing the camera, or who cannot say which way it is going, FAILS this entry. Nothing in this file asked about it before 2026-09-09, which is why a front-on side-scroller character shipped. JUDGE IT AT 390 px, NOT AT 1x. The first correction turned the body and left the head at the body angle; it passed every 1x render it was shown in, and at phone width the guide read as travelling while both humans read as standing still looking at the player. A cue that is 2 px on a phone is not a cue.
mustBeRight.detail: Three-quarter, canonical facing RIGHT. The BODY sits about 40 degrees off strict profile and the HEAD turns further, to about 25 degrees, which is what a walking head does and which is what lets the officer keep the chest plane its cross-strap needs. WHAT CARRIES IT AT PHONE SIZE IS THE HEAD OUTLINE: an asymmetric silhouette with a big smooth cranium behind and a brow, nose, lip and chin in front, the nose projecting about 16 px. Supporting cues, in the order they survive being made small: the hair mass at the BACK with the fringe sweeping forward; the chest plane and its fastening on the leading edge; BOTH feet pointing the way the character travels; the neck, a lit column between jaw and a darker collar, without which the head-and-shoulder mass reads as one lump; the hat brim swung forward, or the toque band running STEEPLY downhill to the back - level over the face, because it must clear the brows, and dropping behind it; the eyes crowded into the front third with the far one foreshortened; and ONE ear, well back. The near side is the wearer right side, so the near arm and leg draw in front. See art-bible.md 7.1.

mustBeRight.feature: cartoon proportions identical to every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires it and docs/content-review.md 6.2 gives the reason: comparison only works if everyone is compared. A verifier shown ONE figure cannot check this and must not be asked to, so the hand-off carries a second figure on the same rig in a different costume. TIGHTENED 2026-09-09 after the repository owner reported the player shoulders as out of proportion and THIS ENTRY HAD SCORED PRESENT ANYWAY. It scored present because it asked only whether two figures matched, and they did - they were equally wrong, both built to a canon whose shoulder row was 54 percent over a measured photograph. An entry that cannot see the widest part of a figure is not measuring proportions, so it now names that measurement, gives the number, gives the reference the number came from, and says which quantity is allowed to differ.
mustBeRight.detail: 6 heads tall, 420 px crown to sole at design resolution, head 70 px. MEASURE THE WIDEST POINT OF EACH FIGURE - not the shoulder line by eye, the widest point, wherever it falls - as a fraction of that figure own crown-to-sole height. AND CHECK THE NECK: every figure must show a column of its own surface between the jaw and the collar, 12 to 13 px at design resolution, about 4 px at 390 px, with the collar DARKER than the column beneath it. A figure whose head sits straight on the shoulders FAILS this entry however well its width measures - that was reported from the live site as "the head is on the torso" and it is most of why the shoulders still looked wrong after their width was corrected. It is derived, not chosen: 0.149 of head height, measured on officer/red-serge-full-figure.jpg, see art-bible.md 7.3. The guide is held to the same column in pelt rather than skin, which is a surface exemption for one non-human artboard and not a licence to draw it neckless. On the shipped art that is 113 px at the waist on a 442 px figure, which is 0.256 of its own height, with the paddle tail excluded because it is held out to one side and is not part of the body. The cap for every character is 116 px, which is 0.276 of height. It is derived, not chosen: an adult in a winter parka in assets/refs/ottawa/rideau-canal-skateway-ice.jpg measures 0.238 of their own height across the shoulders with the arms hanging in, and 0.276 is that plus a deliberate cartoon broadening of about a tenth. A figure at or over 0.30 FAILS this entry however well it matches the figure beside it.
mustBeRight.whatMayDiffer: THE GARMENT, WITHIN THE CAP. A parka genuinely broadens the shoulders and a fitted tunic barely does, so the three costumes measure the beaver 113, the parka 108 and the serge 104 px. A verifier should NOT fail the pair over a few pixels of coat.
mustBeRight.whatMayNotDiffer: THE FIGURE. Crown line, sole line, eye line, the heights of the shoulder, hip, knee and ankle, the size of the hands and of the feet, the head size and the three stroke weights are IDENTICAL between the guide and the player and the officer, because they are the same rig and, for the limbs and hands, literally the same atlas frames. If a verifier can see that one figure head is bigger, its eye line higher or its hands larger, that is the failure this entry is for.

simplifyAway: individual fur strands and the wet-fur parting the photographs show
whiskers - below the 12 px minimum shape at every shipping size
claws as separate digits; three ticks at the paw edge stand in for them
the fine scale grid of the tail, which becomes three cross bands
nostrils, and any modelling inside the nose pad
neverAdd: clothing, a hat, a scarf or an accessory of any kind - the guide is an animal, not a person in a suit
any Indigenous item, pattern, regalia or motif, on the guide or near it (docs/content-review.md)
a national flag, a maple leaf, an emblem or lettering
a felled log, a dam or a construction prop used as a joke about the animal
buck teeth drawn as a comic overbite past the chin, or any other caricature of the animal
a second, smaller or larger proportion than every other character
subjects.whyTheOmissions: The guide exists so the game can be literally Canadian at the points of interest without spending the character creator on a mascot. It stays an animal companion: no costume, no cultural item, no props. Skin colour is the one row of the art bible 7 table that cannot apply to it - its fills are leather, felt, hide and white, not a skin ramp - and that is a recorded exemption for one non-human artboard, not a licence to score any human character the same way.
notes: beaver-upright-winter-gnawing.jpg is the pose reference: a beaver sitting up on its hind legs in snow holding a stick in its forepaws. The design is a cartoon of that stance.
beaver-head-and-forepaws.jpg is backlit through grass and carries a cool cast: it is a GEOMETRY reference for the ear, muzzle and forepaw, and the fur colour was not taken from it alone.
beaver-upright-winter-gnawing.jpg is a dusk exposure and is a colour trap: its fur medians at L 18 and S 6. It was excluded from the pelt measurement and used for pose only.

The incisors are drawn WHITE and real beaver incisors are orange. That is a labelled legibility exaggeration recorded in assets/style/guide.md 3, not an oversight: at ship size a tooth is about 4 px wide and orange enamel on a felt snout pad is two warm tans touching.

subjects.subject: The Canadian Museum for Human Rights, Winnipeg
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower, chateau-frontenac, town-clock and cn-tower.
expectedBlindAnswer: Musee canadien pour les droits de la personne
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS ALLOWED TO DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and it is the only render in this level that may.
It is a single non-repeating POI hero drawing one specific building whose stack - a stepped mountain of
pale limestone, a curved blue-green glass shell wrapping its left flank, and a tapering glazed spire
with an open steel lattice above it - is shared by no other building this game will draw. A verifier
who cannot name it is reporting a defect in the drawing.
IT IS ALSO THE LEVEL'S ONLY ANCHOR THAT CAN. `winnipeg-riverwalk` is two repeating parallax tiles and
is asked for a promenade and never for a city. So Winnipeg as a place rests on this render alone. If
this landmark stops identifying, the level stops being identifiable, and no work on the tiles buys it back.

mustBeRight.feature: a tall tapering spire rising from the highest point of the stone, glazed below and an OPEN steel lattice above
mustBeRight.why: It is the top of the silhouette and the first thing a person uses to find the building on a skyline. A solid spire, or one that is glass all the way up, is a different building.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on winnipeg/cmhr-elevation-from-the-river.jpg against the building's width B (x 65..1140 at the foot, so B = 1075 px): the spire rises 0.393 B above the stone peak, is glazed for the lower 0.253 and open steel for the upper 0.140, is 0.135 B wide at its foot and 0.050 B at the lattice, and its axis is 0.402 B from the left edge. The lattice is drawn as three legs and cross bracing - a rhythm, not a mesh - because a true lattice at ship size is noise.

mustBeRight.feature: a large curved glazed shell wrapping the LEFT flank and front, cresting BELOW the stone peak
mustBeRight.why: It is the museum's second signature and the relationship that goes wrong first. A shell that crests above the stone reads as the top of the building and the whole massing inverts.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: the shell is 0.321 B across and crests 0.465 B above the foot, which is about a tenth of B BELOW the stone peak at 0.567 B. Its ribs are DIAGONAL and converge toward the crest, with two horizontal rings across them: vertical mullions turned it into an egg twice before the diagonals went in. Blue-green glass, the `ice` ramp, measured at hsl(203,41%,80%) sunlit against ice-base's hsl(202,52%,78%).

mustBeRight.feature: a mass of pale buff limestone built as CANTED wedges with sloped tops, stepping down to the right
mustBeRight.why: The stone is most of the building's area, and it is what stops the museum reading as a glass box with a mast on it. Stacked rectangles in pale stone read as an office block; the wedges lean.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED: peak 0.567 B above the foot, right-hand steps at 0.366 B and 0.140 B, overall height : width 0.953. Six wedges, each with its shade on its RIGHT edge because the key light is upper left.

mustBeRight.feature: TYNDALL LIMESTONE, and not the sandstone of Parliament Hill
mustBeRight.why: This game now has two landmarks faced in pale stone. Drawn in one ramp they become the same material and two levels lose their difference - the same argument that keeps brick off Parliament Hill and stone off the Chateau.
mustBeRight.detail: `limestone` is its own ramp, base #a99789 = hsl(26,16%,60%), authored from the median of 240x400 px of sunlit wall at (620,700) on winnipeg/cmhr-elevation-from-the-river.jpg. Nepean sandstone's base is hsl(33,41%,58%): the same lightness at two and a half times the saturation.

mustBeRight.feature: no windows in rows, anywhere
mustBeRight.why: It is a museum with almost no punched openings, and a grid of windows is the single fastest way to turn this drawing into a generic civic building.
mustBeRight.detail: Two canted glazing slots cut across the stone and one dark glazed band at the foot for the entrance. Nothing else. No storey banding, no sills, no mullioned grid.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands on a low terrace, not on a plaza and not on a hill
mustBeRight.detail: A limestone plinth wall with a thin grass verge either side, matching the level's own theme.ground so the landmark and the promenade are the same ground. winnipeg/cmhr-at-the-forks.jpg and winnipeg/cmhr-from-the-forks-tower.jpg both show the terrace.

the shell's individual glazing panels: six diagonal ribs and two rings replace several hundred triangles
the ramps, stairs and the reflecting pool at the entrance

the roof plant, the aerials and the window-cleaning davits
the banner hung on the stone in two of the references: it is really there, it changes with the exhibition, and it is lettering

a flag or a flagpole on the building

punched windows in storey rows on the stone
a cross, a spire finial or any religious emblem on the tower: the spire is a glazed lift and stair shaft and reads as a steeple the moment anything is put on top of it
the Golden Boy, the Manitoba Legislative Building or any other Winnipeg landmark in the same frame
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement: the level names seven and depicts none (docs/content-review.md 1)

PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise

The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 1000 x 1040 and passed at both
