subjects.subject: A paved riverside promenade with a low stone parapet, under a city skyline
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the skyline above the promenade, the promenade placed 180 px below the skyline tile's top edge (world y 800 against 620). Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920) rather than laying them side by side, and draw the promenade over the skyline where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. Neither file answers the subject alone: a skyline with no ground is a skyline, and a pavement with nothing behind it is a pavement. `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'skyline', nearMatch: 'plaza', nearTop: 180 })`. THE RIVER IS NOT IN THIS COMPOSITE: it lives on layer-30-riverbank, which is the third tile and is not part of this subject, so the parapet reads as a parapet and not as a riverbank.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this one has teeth: the skyline tile repeats every 1800 px and the promenade
every 1920, so neither may carry a recognisable building. Every tower on the skyline is a plain mass
and every object on the promenade is a type. A verifier who names Winnipeg from these two tiles would
be reporting a defect, not a pass.
THE LIST IS WIDE ON THE PLAIN WORDS AND NARROW ON EVERYTHING ELSE, which is the amendment
`toronto-trail` and `rideau-canal-skateway` both needed and which is stated once here rather than
`a road`, `a street`, `a boardwalk` and `a quay` do not. `a boardwalk` is refused deliberately -
picture shows. `a road`, `a street`, `a boardwalk` and `a quay` do not. `a boardwalk` is refused
deliberately - Halifax's tile IS a timber boardwalk, this one is stone slabs, and a list that accepted
both would stop being able to tell them apart.
WHERE WINNIPEG ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `human-rights-museum`, a separate non-repeating POI hero. The
promenade is where the player walks; the museum is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: a pavement of large stone SLABS in courses, not planks and not asphalt
mustBeRight.why: It is what makes this a promenade rather than a road or a boardwalk, and it is the one thing Halifax's equivalent tile got wrong: `grey weathered planking` is an equally true description of a concrete pavement, and the drawing obeyed it exactly.
mustBeRight.detail: Two shallow courses of small setts on a 34 px module at the parapet foot, then four courses of large slabs on a 160 px module staggered half a slab per course, graded so the near courses are much taller. Joints are quiet - path-base at 0.7 - because at the weight of the course lines they turn the pavement into brickwork, which is what the first attempt looked like.

mustBeRight.feature: a low stone parapet with piers along the far side
mustBeRight.why: It is the edge that says the promenade stands above something, and it is the reason the walkway is a promenade and not a footpath in a field.
mustBeRight.detail: A limestone wall with a sunlit coping and a pier every 240 px, eight to the tile.

mustBeRight.feature: street trees in EARLY AUTUMN, gold and green together
mustBeRight.why: The season separates this level from the two winter levels and the two summer ones, and a level whose trees are uniformly green is summer.
mustBeRight.detail: Three trees per tile, two in gold and one still green, drawn as three-tone rounded canopies. Never a leaf texture.

mustBeRight.feature: people to the same cartoon proportions as every other character
mustBeRight.why: CLAUDE.md requires identical cartoon proportions for every character, and background figures in a parallax tile are where that rule is quietly broken first.
mustBeRight.detail: Six heads tall, the same proportion canon as the player, drawn at about 165 px rather than the player's 420 because they stand at the parapet across the promenade. No outline - outlines are for characters. NO CULTURAL MARKER OF ANY KIND: docs/content-review.md 3.3, outcome 2.

mustBeRight.feature: a city skyline of plain masses behind, in concrete and glass
mustBeRight.detail: Twenty-one rectangular masses with flat tops, arrises, storey banding and plant enclosures, standing out of an opaque haze band. Rhythm and massing only, never a grid of window panes.

simplifyAway: individual windows on the towers: a horizontal band rhythm, never a grid of panes
the individual leaves, and any bark texture on the trunks
traffic, cycle traffic and street signs
drainage, tactile paving and kerb ramps
the joint pattern of the parapet coping below 6 px
neverAdd: any named or recognisable building drawn into either of these two REPEATING tiles, and the Canadian Museum for Human Rights above all: it is required on the `human-rights-museum` subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
the Golden Boy or the Manitoba Legislative Building, in any form, including on the skyline
any lettering, signage or wordmark, in either language
a bridge with a single inclined pylon: the Esplanade Riel is a real and recognisable structure and a repeating tile may not carry one
snow, or bare winter trees: this level is early autumn
mountains on the horizon: this city is on a river plain
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement
notes: winnipeg/winnipeg-skyline-and-cmhr.jpg is the massing reference for the tower rhythm: a mid-rise
downtown with a few taller towers and one blue-green glass slab, which is what the tile draws as

winnipeg/cmhr-from-esplanade-riel.jpg and winnipeg/cmhr-from-the-forks-tower.jpg are the references
for the riverbank planting and the promenade furniture.
THE RIVER LIVES ON A THIRD TILE. layer-30-riverbank.svg carries the far bank and the open water and is
NOT part of this subject or of any other: it is a repeating background band that the low preset drops,

subjects.subject: A wooden prairie grain elevator beside a railway track
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is a POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT MAY NOT DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and the reason is the same one that governs `pier-21`.
Every wooden prairie elevator carries its company's name and its town's name painted across the crib -
PIONEER and CHAMBERLAIN on the reference this one is drawn from, SASKATCHEWAN and SINTALUTA on the
second - and `make verify-art` refuses any render source containing a <text> element, because a name
drawn into the picture defeats every byte-level leak check in the hand-off. So the elevator ships
blank, and what is left is the STANDARD PLAN that stood in a thousand prairie towns: a type.
`Saskatchewan`, `the Prairies` and any town name are therefore NOT in the accepted list and the gate
MUST NOT reward them. A verifier who names a province from this render has inferred it; a verifier who
says `a grain elevator` has seen what is drawn.
THE CONSEQUENCE IS STRUCTURAL AND IS STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED. Level 7 is a REGION,
not a town, and nothing in its art is asked to name a place - not this hero and not
`prairie-rail-line`. That is a deliberate choice and not an omission: the level's subject is Modern
Canada and its setting is the plains, and the only honest anchor a plains level has is the type.

mustBeRight.feature: a tall gable-roofed CRIB, well over twice as tall as it is wide
mustBeRight.why: It is the whole silhouette. Below about 1 : 2 the building stops being an elevator and becomes a barn.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED TWICE AND THE TWO AGREE. On prairie-rail/grain-elevator-chamberlain.jpg the crib is 380 px wide and 870 px from the ground to the gable apex; on prairie-rail/grain-elevator-sintaluta-elevation.jpg the same figures are 270 and 615. HEIGHT : WIDTH = 2.29 and 2.28. The shipped art is 280 x 638 = 2.28. Gable rise 0.30 of the crib width, which is the MEAN of the two references' 0.25 and 0.35 and is recorded as a mean rather than left looking like a measurement.

mustBeRight.feature: a CUPOLA straddling the ridge, narrower than the crib and rising well above it
mustBeRight.why: It is the head house that carries the leg, it is the second thing a person recognises, and a gabled box with no cupola is a shed.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on the Sintaluta elevation, which is the near-orthographic one: the cupola is 0.30 of the crib width across and rises 0.44 of the crib width above the gable apex. It has its own small gable roof and a vent above it.

mustBeRight.feature: a LOW driveway annex along one side, with a shed roof falling away from the crib and an opening a truck drives into
mustBeRight.why: The tall-box-and-long-low-shed pair is the elevator's whole asymmetry. A crib standing alone reads as a tower.
mustBeRight.detail: 1.45 crib widths long, 1.00 crib widths tall where it meets the crib and 0.52 at the far end. Chamberlain's apparent length is 1.68 crib widths and is NOT used: that photograph is taken close and low and the annex recedes hard away from the camera, so its apparent length is a projection.

mustBeRight.feature: painted timber in a strong red oxide, with contrasting ochre trim on the gable edge and the eaves
mustBeRight.why: It is what says painted wooden building rather than concrete terminal, and the trim band is the elevator's one piece of colour.
mustBeRight.detail: `oxide` is its own palette ramp, base #91301c = hsl(11,68%,34%), authored as the HSL midpoint of the two large measured faces on the Chamberlain reference: the sunlit annex at hsl(8,73%,36%) and the shaded crib gable at hsl(13,63%,32%). NOT `brick`, whose base is hsl(17,52%,44%) - eight degrees more orange, sixteen points less saturated and ten points lighter, which turns a painted elevator into a masonry wall. Trim is `brass`.

mustBeRight.feature: a loading spout reaching out from the cupola toward the track side
mustBeRight.detail: A slanted steel tube from the head house down to a spout head, over a low track-side annex. It is what the building is FOR, and without it the crib is a grain bin with a hat.

mustBeRight.feature: it stands in gravel beside a rail, not on grass and not on a street
mustBeRight.detail: A ballast apron with a siding rail across the foot of the file, and weeds at its back edge. prairie-rail/grain-elevator-govan-and-track.jpg shows exactly this relationship from beside the line.

simplifyAway: the board-and-batten boarding: it is a surface pattern, and art-bible section 1 forbids drawing one
the man-lift, the ladders, the catwalks and the guy wires
the external cyclone and dust pipe on the Chamberlain reference: it is unusual to that building and reads as a chimney
the individual sash bars of the crib windows: one dark pane with an ochre head
the steel bins, the driveway scale and the seed-cleaning plant that stand beside most surviving elevators

the company name and the town name painted across the crib, and the star or shield device beside them: they are the two most identifying things on the real building and this project draws no lettering
neverAdd: any lettering, wordmark, company name, town name or number, in either language
an invented company name or an invented device in place of the real one: art-bible's `drop, never substitute`, and an approximated livery mark is worse than none
a concrete terminal, a slip-form silo or a row of steel bins as the main mass: those are the modern replacement and are a different building
a barn: no hip roof, no cupola with louvres on a wide low mass, no hayloft door
mountains or foothills on the horizon behind it: that is level 8's picture, not this one
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement
notes: prairie-rail/grain-elevator-chamberlain.jpg is CC0 and is the building this is drawn from: the
surviving Pioneer elevator at Chamberlain, Saskatchewan. It is the reference for the livery, the trim,
the driveway and the arrangement, and for the crib's height : width. It is taken close and from below,
so it is NOT the reference for the annex's length.
prairie-rail/grain-elevator-sintaluta-elevation.jpg is the near-orthographic one and is the reference
for the cupola's proportions and for the second, agreeing, height : width measurement.
prairie-rail/grain-elevator-govan-and-track.jpg shows a surviving elevator beside the main line with
the prairie running to the horizon behind it, and is the reference for the SETTING and for the fact
that the gable end and the annex flank really are both visible from beside the track.
prairie-rail/grain-elevators-mossleigh-elevation.jpg and prairie-rail/prairie-elevator-from-the-train.jpg
are the cross-checks: three elevators in a row and one seen from a moving train, both near-orthographic.
PLACEMENT FLOOR: do not draw this landmark below 300 px wide anywhere the player is meant to recognise
it. The verifier's floor from Ottawa, adopted rather than re-derived. As a DRAWING OBSERVATION and
explicitly not an identification: at 250 px the crib, the cupola, the annex and the spout are all still
separable and the trim still reads as trim.
The two-size test in art-bible section 5 was run at the shipping size of 900 x 1000 and passed at both
probes. The measured saving from pinning it to 1x is 13.73 MiB -> 3.43 MiB of decoded texture.

subjects.subject: A single-track railway line running across open prairie
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the fields ABOVE the railbed and the railbed drawn over them where they overlap, which is the order the level uses. In world coordinates the railbed tile's top edge is 210 px ABOVE the fields tile's top edge (world y 800 against 1010), so the offset is NEGATIVE: `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'fields', nearMatch: 'railbed', nearTop: -210 })`. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920) rather than laying them side by side. Neither file answers the subject alone: a track with nothing behind it is a track anywhere, and a field with no track is a field.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both tiles repeat - 1800 and 1920 - so neither may carry anything that identifies a
place, and in particular neither carries a grain elevator: that is the level's only non-repeating
anchor and it lives on `grain-elevator`. A verifier who names a province from these two tiles would be
reporting a defect.
`railroad` and `railroad track` are accepted alongside `railway`, and this is the amendment
`toronto-trail` needed after a blind pass failed on `bicycle` when only `bike` and `cycle` were listed.
The rule stated once: an expectedBlindAnswer list is a VOCABULARY for one picture, and a list that
omits a plain word for the thing drawn measures the verifier's diction rather than the art. `a road`,
`a path`, `a tram line` and `a level crossing` alone do not pass: the last one names the furniture and
not the line.
THE PRAIRIE IS NOT ASKED FOR. `across the prairie` is in the list because a verifier who says it is not
wrong, and it is NOT required: flat farmland under a big sky is flat farmland under a big sky, and the
art may not be scored on an inference.

mustBeRight.feature: two rails on timber ties over a ballast shoulder, running the full width
mustBeRight.why: It is the subject. One rail is a fence, and rails without ties are a pipeline.
mustBeRight.detail: Forty ties on a 48 px period - 1920 / 48 = 40 exactly, so the rhythm survives the tile seam - two rails, and a ballast shoulder drawn as scattered chips rather than a texture fill. The near rail head is the level's ground line.

mustBeRight.feature: a red-edged white CROSSBUCK and a two-lens flashing-light mast at a gravel crossing
mustBeRight.why: It is the one object in this level that says RAILWAY without a word on it, which is exactly what a project that draws no lettering needs, and it is what stops the track reading as a tramway or a mine road.
mustBeRight.detail: Two white boards crossed at about 26 degrees with a red border, on a white mast, under a black backing board carrying two red lenses. NO LETTERING: a real Canadian crossbuck carries words and this one carries none, which is a deliberate omission and not an oversight. A gravel section road crosses behind it and the crossing deck runs over the ties.

mustBeRight.feature: timber telegraph poles with crossarms and drooping wires, on a strict repeating period
mustBeRight.why: The level's locomotion is `train` and the camera does all the work: the pole rhythm is what makes movement legible, and it is the oldest visual shorthand there is for a railway on a plain.
mustBeRight.detail: Four poles on a 480 px period - 1920 / 480 = 4 exactly - each with a crossarm, four glass insulators and three drooping catenary wires into the next bay.

mustBeRight.feature: harvested field in SWATHS, laid at a slight angle to the track
mustBeRight.why: Parallel bands alone read as a striped rug. A cut crop lying in rows at an angle is what a prairie field looks like from a train, and it is what makes this farmland rather than grassland.
mustBeRight.detail: Fourteen long cut rows across the fields tile, each with its own shadow line, over bands of standing swath, cut stubble and a grass headland. Straw is the `felt` ramp, measured at hsl(38,63%,33%) on prairie-rail/prairie-harvest-and-shelterbelt.jpg.

mustBeRight.feature: a poplar shelterbelt in broken clumps with real gaps, not a continuous hedge
mustBeRight.detail: Four clumps to the tile with gaps between them. A continuous row reads as a hedge and closes the horizon, which is the one thing a prairie level cannot afford.

simplifyAway: the rail's web and foot profile: two flat bars with a lit top arris
tie plates, spikes, joint bars and ballast between the ties
the insulators' individual caps below 8 px
the fence's staples and the wire's sag between posts
the crossing signal's bell, its gate arm and its cabinet
neverAdd: a grain elevator ON EITHER OF THESE TWO REPEATING TILES: it is required on the `grain-elevator` subject and forbidden here, and the reason is the tiling, not the building
any lettering, number plate, whistle post, mile board or signage, in either language
a locomotive or rolling stock: the player IS the train in this level, and a drawn train in the frame makes the player a passenger of something that is already on screen
overhead electrification, a catenary mast or a third rail: this is a diesel-worked prairie branch
mountains or foothills on the horizon: that is level 8's picture
a second track, a turnout or a signal gantry: it is a single-track line
any depiction of a person, a pattern or an object belonging to any nation named in this level's territory statement
notes: prairie-rail/grain-elevator-govan-and-track.jpg is the primary reference: single track, ballast
shoulder, a siding, a wire fence and the prairie running flat to the horizon, all in one frame.
prairie-rail/prairie-harvest-and-shelterbelt.jpg is the reference for the swaths, the stubble bands
and the shelterbelt line; prairie-rail/prairie-elevator-from-the-train.jpg is the reference for what
the level's own viewpoint actually looks like, because it was taken from one.
prairie-rail/prairie-freight-train-at-dawn.jpg shows a freight beside an elevator and is the reference
for the track's relationship to the buildings. It is NOT a colour reference: it is a winter dawn.
THE SKY AND THE FAR HORIZON ARE NOT PART OF THIS SUBJECT. layer-10-sky.svg and layer-20-horizon.svg are
drawn, credited and shipped and are asked no question: one is a flat field with clouds and the other is
a distant shelterbelt and two farmsteads, and neither has a feature that could identify anything.

subjects.subject: A working cattle ranch in the Alberta foothills: a red board-sided gable barn with a louvred ridge cupola, a peeled-log corral and a work horse. Drawn from the Bar U Ranch National Historic Site at Longview, Alberta.
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. scripts/lib/art-handoff.mjs builds it with `singleSource()`, the same builder as peace-tower, chateau-frontenac, town-clock, cn-tower, human-rights-museum and grain-elevator.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT MAY NOT DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and the reason is the one that governs `pier-21` and
`grain-elevator`. A ranch barn is a standard timber building type that stood across western North
America; nothing drawn says which country it is in, let alone which province. `Alberta`, `the
foothills` and any town name are NOT in the accepted list and the gate MUST NOT reward them. A
verifier who names a province here has inferred it from project context, which is the mistake the
Ottawa canal subject made and had to be amended for.
WHAT IT MAY DEMAND IS THE WORD RANCH, and that IS a measurement rather than a preference. The render
draws a barn AND a corral AND a horse inside the corral, and those three together are what separates
a ranch from a farm. So `a red barn`, `a barn` and `a farm` alone do NOT pass: an answer naming only
the building is a true report that the corral and the horse did not carry, which is information about
the drawing and is what this gate is for. Every accepted phrase names the enclosure or the word ranch.
THE CONSEQUENCE IS STRUCTURAL. Level 8 is a REGION and nothing in its art is asked to name a place -
not this hero and not `alberta-foothills-rangeland`. The Rocky Mountain front IS in the level, on
layer 20, and is not a graded subject: it repeats and the low preset drops it.

mustBeRight.feature: red-oxide painted timber walls
mustBeRight.why: Barn red on a gable barn is the strongest single colour cue this subject has.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED 2026-09-09, six medians across three references: work-horse-barn-elevation.jpg at (500,715) hsl(4,56%,21%) and (900,760) hsl(4,50%,21%); work-horse-barn-gable-end.jpg at (1080,430) hsl(7,54%,18%) and (1250,430) hsl(3,52%,22%); percheron-at-the-barn-wall.jpg at (60,250) hsl(8,51%,26%) and (360,230) hsl(5,37%,23%). Median hsl(5,51%,21%). All three photographs are late evening or overcast, so the sample sits about 13 points of lightness below the material. Drawn in the `oxide` ramp - the prairie grain elevator's own red-oxide paint on the same painted timber - and NO NEW RAMP WAS ADDED: corrected for the photographs' light the sample lands five degrees of hue and eight points of saturation from oxide-base. Not `brick`, which is masonry, and not `wood`, which is bare timber.

mustBeRight.feature: a gable end facing the viewer, and a long flank running off it
mustBeRight.detail: The gable rise is 0.735 of the eave height. MEASURED at the LEFT end of work-horse-barn-elevation.jpg, where the eave line is horizontal across 785 px (slope +0.010), which proves the camera sits at eave height and makes the vertical readings there free of foreshortening: ridge 528, eave 692, foundation 915. THE PLAN WIDTH IS NOT MEASURED. It is 1.47 of the eave height, DERIVED from a 12:12 pitch, because no reference in the set gives a gable end free of foreshortening; that is written here rather than left looking like accuracy. The drawn flank is 1.45 eave heights against a real 3.6, shortened so the corral has somewhere to stand - the same decision, for the same reason, as the grain elevator's annex.

mustBeRight.feature: a louvred cupola on the ridge
mustBeRight.why: The ridge vent separates a barn from a house or a machine shed at any scale, and it is the top of the silhouette.
mustBeRight.detail: A small louvred box centred on the ridge over the flank, about 0.43 of the eave height wide, rising about 0.22 of the eave height above the ridge, with its own low pyramid roof and four horizontal louvre bars.

mustBeRight.feature: a run of small white-framed windows along the flank
mustBeRight.detail: Five, evenly spaced: rhythm replacing count (art-bible section 5 rule 3). MEASURED window height 0.233 of the eave height and sill 0.31 of the eave height above the foot, off seven windows on the primary reference. The white frames are the barn's only bright trim and are what stop the flank reading as a blank wall.

mustBeRight.feature: a large sliding door on the gable end
mustBeRight.detail: White-framed, on a visible head track, about 0.4 of the gable-end width, reaching from the foot to a little over half the eave height, with a diagonal ledge brace.

mustBeRight.feature: a peeled-log post-and-rail corral in front of the barn, and a braced gate in it
mustBeRight.why: THIS IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THE SUBJECT A RANCH. Without it the render is a barn, which is why every accepted answer names the enclosure or the word ranch.
mustBeRight.detail: Round peeled posts on a regular rhythm with three round rails, in the `wood` ramp from log-rail-fence.jpg, and one gate with a single diagonal brace. Never sawn pickets, never wire, never a stone wall.

mustBeRight.feature: one horse standing inside the corral
mustBeRight.detail: A grey Percheron, from percheron-at-the-barn-wall.jpg. Drawn at 118 px at the withers against the barn's 300 px eave: the eave is about 4.2 m, so 1 m is 71 px and a 1.65 m horse is 117. The animal is at the BUILDING's scale, not at a scale that would read better, which is the only way the barn keeps its measured proportions.

mustBeRight.feature: a grey weathered shingle roof
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED hsl(20,5%,50%), hsl(26,3%,44%) and hsl(0,1%,50%) across three references against `path`'s base at hsl(31,7%,51%), so the roof is drawn in `path` and no grey was added. Not green, not red, not metal.

simplifyAway: the board-and-batten battens and every shingle course beyond an even rhythm
the hay-track hardware, the ladders and the lightning rods
the farm machinery that stands in the yard in every reference
the corral's wire, staples and gate hardware
the horse's dapples, feather and harness
the foundation's stonework, which is one flat band
the Red Ensign that flies over the ranch office in two references: it is a historical flag and drawing it would make the render a claim about a date
neverAdd: any lettering, number or date, in either language
a ranch brand, a company device or a gate sign - an approximated brand is worse than none (art-bible's 'drop, never substitute')
a grain elevator or a silo: that is level 7's landmark and one here would move this level's identity onto another level's subject
a gambrel, hip or round roof - the reference is a straight gable, and a gambrel is the American barn silhouette this one is not
a windmill, a weather vane or a cupola finial
mountains INSIDE this file: the Rocky Mountain front is a parallax layer, and a hero carrying it would put the level's landform on the one render that never repeats
a person, a wagon or a saddle: the rancher is an NPC nobody has placed, and a hero is not where a character goes
notes: The reference set is eight CC BY 2.0 photographs, seven of them from one visit to the Bar U Ranch National Historic Site by one Flickr photographer. LICENCE FIRST, AND IT COST THE BEST FILES: every dedicated barn elevation on Wikimedia Commons - `Bar U Ranch saddle horse barn east side`, `west side`, `work horse barn` - is CC BY-SA 4.0, and the site panoramas are CC BY-SA 3.0, which ADR-0004 excludes for its ShareAlike condition. That is why the measurement leans on a flank view taken in evening light rather than on an orthographic elevation, and why the plan width is a derivation.

subjects.subject: Rolling foothills rangeland: grass ridges with tree bluffs in the folds, a wire fence on wooden posts, cattle grazing and a two-track ranch road.
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the rangeland drawn OVER the foothills, which is the order the level uses. In world coordinates the rangeland tile's top edge is 60 px ABOVE the foothills tile's top edge (world y 880 against 940), so the offset is NEGATIVE: `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'foothills', nearMatch: 'rangeland', nearTop: -60 })`. This is the SECOND negative offset in that table, after prairie-rail-line, and for the same reason: the foreground tile spends its top 250 rows on fence posts and wire that stand UP into the sky. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920) rather than laying them side by side. Neither file answers the subject alone: ridges with no fence and no stock are hills, and a fence with nothing behind it is a fence. THE MOUNTAIN FRONT IS NOT IN THIS COMPOSITE: it lives on layer-20, which is a third tile and is deliberately out of scope, so the answer is a landform these two tiles actually show.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE, and this one has teeth. The foothills tile repeats every 1800 px and the
rangeland every 1920, so neither may carry anything that identifies a place: there is no building of
any kind on either, and the cattle and the fence are types. A verifier who names a province from
these two tiles would be reporting a defect rather than passing.
`the Rockies`, `the Rocky Mountains` and any mountain answer are NOT in this list, and their absence
is deliberate: the mountain front is drawn, on a third tile, and is not in this render. A contract
that accepted it here would reward a memory of the level rather than a reading of the picture.
THE LIST IS WIDE ON THE PLAIN WORDS AND NARROW ON EVERYTHING ELSE, which is the amendment
toronto-trail and rideau-canal-skateway both needed. `farmland` and `prairie` pass because a person
looking at ridges, stock and a fence may honestly say either and would not be wrong about what is
drawn. `a field`, `a park`, `a lawn` and `a golf course` do not: they miss the stock, the fence or
the relief, and those three are the picture.

mustBeRight.feature: rolling grass ridges, one behind another
mustBeRight.detail: Three ridge lines in the `pasture` ramp, each a rolling curve rather than a straight band, with coulees cut down the near faces. Relief is the difference between this subject and the flat farmland of prairie-rail-line, and it is what a verifier is reading.

mustBeRight.feature: dark tree bluffs in the folds of the ridges
mustBeRight.detail: Aspen and spruce clumps in the `pine` ramp, scattered along the ridge feet and in the coulees, as rounded lobes and spires. Never a continuous forest edge.

mustBeRight.feature: a wire fence on wooden posts, running across the whole tile
mustBeRight.why: The post rhythm is what makes movement legible at a horse's speed, and a fence is what tells a viewer this grass is worked rather than wild.
mustBeRight.detail: Posts on an exact divisor of the 1920 px tile so the rhythm does not break at the seam, three wires, and the posts standing UP above the grass horizon into transparent sky.

mustBeRight.feature: cattle grazing
mustBeRight.detail: Hereford - red body, white face, white topline and stockings - from rangeland-cattle-and-wire-fence.jpg. Three per tile, at the grass horizon, small. They are a TYPE and not a herd portrait.

mustBeRight.feature: a two-track ranch road along the ground line
mustBeRight.detail: Two pale wheel tracks in the `felt` ramp with grass between them, on the level's ground polyline. Never a paved road, never a kerb, never a marking.

mustBeRight.feature: yellow-green grass rather than lawn green
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED hsl(75,35%,38%), hsl(83,18%,36%) and hsl(79,40%,29%) across two references. Drawn in the `pasture` ramp, which was ADDED for this level because all three measurements fall OUTSIDE `grass`'s own hue span of 94 to 114 degrees - the same test that kept prairie straw inside `felt` and the museum's glazing inside `ice`.

simplifyAway: every blade, tussock detail and seed head below 12 px
the wire's sag between posts, and the staples
the cattle's ear tags, horns and individual markings
the ruts, gravel and puddles in the two-track
the fence's corner braces and gates
neverAdd: any building at all - a barn, a shed, a house, a windmill or a grain elevator. These are repeating tiles and the level's only non-repeating anchor is `ranch-barn`
a mountain range: it is on layer-20 and this composite is deliberately not asked about it
any lettering, sign or number
a paved road, a power line or a vehicle
a person, and any cultural marker on anything
notes: SCOPED AS A LANDFORM AND NOT A PLACE, which is the whole reason this entry has the shape it does. See `ranch-barn`'s note for what that costs the level.

subjects.subject: Canada Place, Vancouver: the cruise-ship terminal and convention centre, five white fabric sails on masts over a long two-level pier building standing on piles in Burrard Inlet.
subjects.renderRecipe: Rasterise the file on its own at 1x. It is the POI hero and this is the subject it answers. `singleSource()`. The file is 1000 x 800 and its bottom 280 rows are deliberately empty, so the rasterised subject is a building floating above the foot of the frame; that is not a defect and the reason is in the file's own title.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: THIS SUBJECT IS ALLOWED TO DEMAND A PLACE NAME, and it is the only render in this level that may. It
is a single non-repeating POI hero drawing one specific building whose five white fabric sails on a
long low pier are shared by nothing else this game will ever draw. A verifier who cannot place it is
reporting a defect in the drawing. `vancouver-seawall` is two repeating tiles and is asked for a
waterfront path and never for a city, so Vancouver as a place rests on this render alone.
AND THE BUILDING'S OWN NAME IS NOT IN THE LIST, WHICH IS A DEFECT IN THE HARNESS AND NOT IN THE ART.
`leakTokens` takes every word of four letters or more out of `id` and `expectedBlindAnswer` and
refuses any handed-over text that contains one; the briefing the hand-off writes asks the identifier
to name a real, named p-l-a-c-e or thing. The building's name contains that noun, so writing it here
would turn make verify-art red on a hand-off that leaks nothing - and the subject id is `five-sails`
rather than the building's name for exactly the same reason.
WHAT IS SCORED INSTEAD is the CITY, which the same answer almost always carries, and `five sails`,
which is what the building is popularly called and is the count its own architecture is named for.
The residual risk is stated plainly: a verifier who writes the building's name AND NOTHING ELSE is
scored a miss while being exactly right. The fix is one line and is routed rather than worked around:
reword the briefing to ask for `a real, named building or landmark`. This entry is amended the day
that lands. `pier-21`'s note stated this rule first; this is its most expensive instance.

mustBeRight.feature: exactly five white fabric sails
mustBeRight.why: The count is the identification. Art-bible section 5 rule 3 lets a repeated detail's number differ from the reference; here the number IS the feature, and the building is popularly called by it.
mustBeRight.detail: Five sharp peaks in a row on one continuous white fabric mass, in the `white` ramp. Four reads as a marquee and six as a circus tent; neither is this building.

mustBeRight.feature: asymmetric sails: a steep concave rise on the left to a sharp peak, then a long shallow sweep down to the right
mustBeRight.why: This is the whole shape. The first build drew five symmetric cones and they read as tents.
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED on five-sails-close.jpg: between the first and second masts the fabric bottoms out at y 700 against peaks at y 300 and a deck at y 1100 - 42 per cent of the drop, NOT the whole of it. A valley that reaches the deck separates the sails into individual tents; a valley at 0.42 keeps them one roof with five peaks.

mustBeRight.feature: the sails stand on a long, low, two-level white building
mustBeRight.detail: MEASURED against H = the sail peak to the waterline, in one column at the near end of canada-place-from-the-west.jpg: sails 0.384 H, the deck-edge zone 0.070 H, the two-level block 0.411 H, the piles and their shadow 0.135 H, and the mast spacing 0.384 H, so a sail is as wide as it is tall. The block is longer than the sail row and reads as a pier, not a hall.

mustBeRight.feature: the building stands on piles over open water
mustBeRight.why: It is a pier. A version of this building sitting on a shore is a conference centre and not this one.
mustBeRight.detail: A dark under-deck shadow, a rhythm of piles below it, and water at the foot. Its base does not touch the bottom of the frame.

mustBeRight.feature: stay cables fanning down to the right of every mast
mustBeRight.detail: Two or three straight lines from each mast head down to the deck, in the `slate` ramp, from sail-masts-and-rigging.jpg. They are the one dark element on a white building and are what stops the sail row reading as a paper cut-out.

mustBeRight.feature: the National Flag of Canada on the promenade
mustBeRight.detail: ONE flag on a short pole at deck level, where the primary reference shows several. Drawn 46 px wide at design resolution; the art bible's floor is 40, below which a flag stops being a flag. The leaf is a bold five-lobe silhouette, not an eleven-point outline.
mustBeRight.whyMasked: DIAGNOSTIC, never gating. This level's subject is Canadian symbols and the flag is the one saturated colour on an otherwise white building, so the honest question is whether the render identifies without it or whether the flag is doing the work. MEASURED against the shipped 1000 x 800 render: the flag's ink occupies x 417-468 and rows 94-121 and its pole runs to row 224, so this rectangle removes the flag and the head of its pole and takes nothing else except a patch of sail fabric behind it - which is stated rather than claimed to be zero. THE FLAG IS DRAWN ONCE RATHER THAN TWICE BECAUSE OF THIS PROBE: the mechanism takes one rectangle, and two flags 370 px apart could not be removed by one without taking a sail with them.

mustBeRight.feature: a glazed colonnade under the promenade deck
mustBeRight.detail: White columns on a regular bay with the recess dark behind them, in `slate` and `ice`. The under-deck is in its own shadow in every reference, and drawing it light makes the pier read as a cruise ship.

simplifyAway: the several hundred fabric panel seams and their catenary cables
the second and third rows of sails behind the first, which produce eight to ten apparent peaks from most angles
the glazing mullions of the convention centre, the hotel block at the west end and the cruise ships alongside
the promenade's lamp standards, bollards, seating and interpretive panels
the flag's eleven-point leaf outline: at 46 px the notches are under 3 px, so the leaf is a bold five-lobe silhouette (art-bible section 5 rule 3)
neverAdd: any lettering or wordmark. The building carries its name in steel letters on its west face in one reference and this project draws no text anywhere
the emblem beside that name, or any logo, funnel mark or shipping livery
a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md section 5.2)
an inuksuk, in any form, for the same reason and under the same open question
a suspension bridge: the Lions Gate is real and a hundred metres of skyline away, and it is this level's fallback anchor rather than a part of this one
a dome, a spire, a clock or a tower on the pier
a sixth sail, and no sail behind another
notes: LICENCE FIRST, and it cost the best files again, for the fifth level running. Every one of Dietmar Rabich's 6720 px views of this building on Wikimedia Commons is CC BY-SA 4.0 and ADR-0004 excludes ShareAlike, so the measurement is made on a 2048 px CC BY 3.0 view and a 4032 px CC BY 2.0 one. The licences were established through the Commons API before anything was downloaded.

subjects.subject: A paved waterfront path along a low sea wall with a white balustrade, open salt water beyond it, benches, lamp standards, conifers and gulls.
subjects.renderRecipe: Composite the two, the seawall drawn OVER the inlet, which is the order the level uses. The seawall tile's top edge is 40 px BELOW the inlet tile's top edge (world y 900 against 860): `twoParallaxTiles({ farMatch: 'inlet', nearMatch: 'seawall', nearTop: 40 })`. Both are repeating parallax tiles, so lay each from x = 0 and REPEAT it to the wider of the two (1800 and 1920). THE SEAM CLOSES HERE, unlike toronto-trail and winnipeg-riverwalk: the inlet tile is opaque from its own top edge and runs to composite y 300, and the seawall tile is opaque from composite y 290, so the two overlap by 10 px and no matte shows between them. The 40 px above the inlet's top edge carries the cedar tops, the lamp heads and the gulls.
expectedBlindAnswerNote: GENERIC ON PURPOSE. Both tiles repeat - 1800 and 1920 - so neither may carry a recognisable building:
the far shore is plain masses and conifers, the two gantry cranes are types, and the ferry and the
bulk carrier are types. A verifier who names a city from these two tiles would be reporting a defect.
EVERY ACCEPTED PHRASE NAMES THE WATER, and that is the line this list draws rather than a preference.
Half of this composite is open salt water and the wall exists because of it, so `a promenade`, `a
park path`, `a paved walkway` and `a boardwalk` alone do NOT pass. Two of those are accepted answers
of `winnipeg-riverwalk`, whose picture is a stone parapet with no open water in it, and a list that
accepted both would stop being able to tell the two subjects apart - which is the reason that entry
gives for refusing `a boardwalk`.
WHERE VANCOUVER ACTUALLY COMES FROM: `five-sails`, a separate non-repeating POI hero. The seawall is
where the player travels; the pier is what says which city.

mustBeRight.feature: open salt water in flat tones, filling the upper half
mustBeRight.detail: Three flat `water` tones and straight ripple bars, never a gradient and never a blur (ADR-0011). MEASURED hsl(204,29%,22%) on canada-place-and-the-north-shore.jpg against water-shade's hsl(210,65%,29%).

mustBeRight.feature: a white balustrade of turned balusters between heavier piers
mustBeRight.why: It is the one piece of furniture that says SEA WALL rather than park railing, and it is what the reference actually has.
mustBeRight.detail: A continuous run of short white balusters under a coping rail, with a broader pier every 208 px, from seawall-path-and-harbour.jpg. Never a steel guardrail, never glass.

mustBeRight.feature: a paved path along the near side of the wall
mustBeRight.detail: Flat `path` tones with joint lines on a rhythm. It is the surface the player travels on and must read as paving rather than as sand or grass.

mustBeRight.feature: a lawn verge with benches on it
mustBeRight.detail: A strip of `grass` between the balustrade and the paving, with timber-slat benches on steel legs. `grass` and not level 8's `pasture`: a mown seaside park lawn is the same material as the lawn on Parliament Hill.

mustBeRight.feature: tall conifers and lamp standards standing up into the sky
mustBeRight.detail: Two western red cedars per tile as stacked dark lobed tiers, and twin-globe lamp standards on a 470 px rhythm. Both stand ABOVE the tile's opaque line into transparent sky, which is why the tile is 430 px tall.

mustBeRight.feature: gulls
mustBeRight.detail: Flat white double-arc shapes in the air, three to seven per tile. They are the one thing that puts the picture at the sea rather than at a lake.

mustBeRight.feature: people with no cultural marker of any kind
mustBeRight.detail: Four background figures on the paving, in the shared proportion canon, drawn from the palette's skin and hair ramps with ordinary clothing (docs/content-review.md section 3.3, outcome 2). No regalia, no pattern, no cultural item, on any of them.

simplifyAway: the balustrade's mouldings, plinths and drainage scuppers
the wave texture, foam and reflections on the water
the far shore's individual buildings, cranes and cars beyond a low band of masses
every leaf, needle and branch: a cedar is stacked lobed tiers
the benches' fixings, the bins and the cycle-lane markings
faces beyond the shared four-cue set on the background figures
neverAdd: any recognisable building on either tile. Both repeat, and the level's only anchor is `five-sails`
a totem pole, in any form, including background, silhouette and icon (docs/content-review.md section 5.2)
an inuksuk, in any form, for the same reason
a canoe, a kayak or any Indigenous watercraft as scenery (OQ-REVIEW-10)
a suspension bridge, a named ship or a named ferry livery
any lettering, sign, hull name or funnel mark
snow: this level is a clear afternoon and two of this game's levels are winter already
notes: The seam closing to the pixel here is worth carrying, because it is the third arrangement this project has tried and the first that needed no hole. halifax-quayside closes at 160 by putting the near tile's first opaque row exactly on the far tile's bottom edge; toronto-trail and winnipeg-riverwalk both leave a band of matte that a third tile fills in the level. This one closes because the far tile is opaque from its own top edge, which is a property of drawing WATER rather than a skyline.

licenceAudit.method: Wikimedia Commons API, prop=imageinfo&iiprop=extmetadata, before download
licenceAudit.note: Recorded here rather than per asset because credits.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and has no field for a licence-check date. The accepted set widened on 2026-09-08 when the architect reconciled the credits enum with ADR-0004 in both directions: public-domain and CC BY 1.0/2.0/2.5/3.0 added, CC-BY-SA-4.0 removed. Three of the six references parked under OQ-ART-06 became fetchable and are now in; the other three are ShareAlike and stay out. See assets/refs/README.md. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the ten Quebec City references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: seven CC0, one public domain (copyright expired, BAnQ), one CC BY 2.0 (Library and Archives Canada) and one CC BY 3.0. Every one is inside the accepted set above. Three ShareAlike candidates that were better photographs - the Dufferin Terrace ice slide in use, the terrace kiosks in winter, and the Chateau after freezing rain - were rejected on licence, not on quality, exactly as three were for Ottawa. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the fifteen Halifax and Toronto references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: five CC0, five public domain, three CC BY 2.0, two CC BY 3.0 and one CC BY 4.0. Every one is inside the accepted set above. The Halifax Town Clock's best photographs and every photograph of the Citadel are CC BY-SA and were rejected on licence, not on quality, for the third level running - and for the Town Clock that cost real quality, because the ShareAlike set includes the only high-resolution near-orthographic elevations. The one CC BY 4.0 file that was available carried the day. Re-run 2026-09-08 for the six beaver references, by the same method and before any of them was downloaded: three public domain, one CC0, one CC BY 2.0 and one CC BY 2.5. CC-BY-2.5 appears in this list for the first time and it is inside the enum the architect settled - the intersection in assets/refs/README.md already contained it, and the list above had simply never had a member of it.
